📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here it was, the big reveal. After years of planning and wrangling, after more than $10 million spent on engineers and lawyers and architects, after all of the rumors and headlines and finger-pointing, the long-awaited presentation was ready to be made.

It has been revealed that about 42 seconds after it started, things went off the rails. A “shitshow,” as multiple people would later describe to Vanity Fair the two-and-a-half-hour meeting on the morning of July 29.

The setting was the Cotillion Ballroom, the chandeliered 4,000-square-foot event space at Upcoming York’s iconic Pierre Hotel, the site of Al Pacino’s blind tango in Scent of a Woman, where the ceilings are 19 feet high, the curtains are golden, and the windows offer views of Central Park’s southeast corner. Seated at round tables were 40 or so of the people with enough disposable income to call the Pierre home, or at least a home: investor Austin Hearst; Tory Burch, the fashion powerhouse; Lois Chiles, the 1970s-era movie star and model. Joining remotely was Michael Eisner, the former Disney CEO, who last year spent $4.3 million to buy a second apartment there and, with it, even more shares in the co-op that owns the Pierre.

In came representatives from the Khashoggi Holding Tech giant out of Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, and the Dorchester Collection, the luxury hotel management firm owned by the Sultan of Brunei. Their proposition was straightforward. Khashoggi wanted to buy the Pierre—the nearly 200-room hotel and all of the apartments too—for $2 billion, less expenses. It was an enormous haul, even for a neighborhood this tony. And it would be all in cash. “The funds are presently available,” a Khashoggi representative promised.

But if the residents with two thirds of the co-op’s shares accepted the offer, everyone would have to move out. Neighbors would be voting, in effect, to force their fellow neighbors from their apartments.

Recent findings suggest that it would be in their best interest, the Dorchester and Khashoggi reps mentioned. The Pierre was a gem, but a tarnished one after 96 summers and thousands of guests. It didn’t have many of the amenities that come standard these days in a five-star hotel. The façade was already undergoing a $22 million overhaul, and there were deeper, systemic problems to solve. The CEO of the manufacturer managing the Pierre publicly complained it was something of a money pit. All of that would change after Khashoggi bought the place, the presenters promised. Dorchester would invest more than $1 billion into the Pierre, giving the landmark building a grand new entrance on 61st Street, a pool in the basement, and structural renovations throughout.

When it was done, the residents would be first in line to buy apartments at the all-new, all-modern Dorchester-managed Pierre, ready to last another century.

It has been revealed that the response in the Cotillion room was instant and not particularly friendly. Some residents had moved in not long ago. Others had spent millions remodeling their apartments. “How are we going to enjoy all the perks of this wonderfully renewed building when we’re forced to sell at a price you determine and we have to buy reconfigured apartments, not our own, at market prices?” asked Tina Beriro, the philanthropist and longtime resident, in a recording of the meeting reviewed by Vanity Fair. Like many of the residents, Beriro, at 85, was only a few years younger than the hotel itself. “Many of us are going to be dead by the time you finish.”.

Recent findings suggest that christopher Cowdray, Dorchester’s white-haired, Zimbabwe-born president, didn’t have an answer. Nor did he provide much of a response when asked what would happen to the more than 400 people who work at the hotel. “In this case, we are still in discussion at the moment,” Cowdray stated, to audible groans.

Sources indicate that “Many employees have worked here 30 and 40 years and are just about to hit retirement,” Burch pointed out, per the recording. “I have people in the elevator crying that they feel like their job is on the line.”.

Recent findings suggest that the questions kept coming. For years, shareholders had begged—and even sued—to find out more about the sale. But the long-promised detailed plans for the Pierre’s purchase were still weeks away, adding to the tension in the Cotillion room. (One source, very much in favor of a sale, later called the decision to make an elaborate presentation to the shareholders without those specifics “idiotic.”).

Sources indicate that “Look, ladies and gentlemen, I’ve been on the board of the Hearst Corporation for over 25 years. Sat on the boards of many corporations, for profit and not for profit. I have never seen anything like this,” Hearst said, his voice cracking. “This is a serious problem that you have presented to the shareholders, and you guys have done a miserable fucking job.”.

One of the many lawyers in the room interrupted him, and they started going at it. Cowdray and the other presenters were escorted out. At one point, the wife of Michael Stern, the 88-year-old chairman of the co-op’s board, tried to offer his resignation on his behalf (which he then turned down). Even by the famously hostile standards of Fresh York City’s high-end co-ops, this was nasty.

Recent findings suggest that ironically, the co-op’s biggest shareholder—the resident with the most at stake in the sale financially—didn’t show up. Howard Lutnick was busy in the Oval Office that day with President Donald Trump in his role as US commerce secretary.

Recent findings suggest that lutnick had bought the Pierre’s 16-room penthouse, its largest apartment, in 2017 for $44 million. If the sale of the Pierre were to go through, Lutnick would get as much as $100 million for the penthouse, even as his neighbors were forced to sell and hundreds of hotel staffers’ jobs were put in jeopardy. Newmark Group—the real estate services firm hired by the Pierre’s board and controlled by Cantor Fitzgerald, the brokerage house previously run by Lutnick—would earn tens of millions more.

Newmark may have a reputation for shepherding major-ticket sales to completion. But in a letter to the Pierre’s board last year, Beriro called the hiring of the Lutnick-linked firm “a blatant conflict of interest,” an allegation sources close to Lutnick and the board deny. One Pierre resident tells me that Lutnick’s involvement is symbolic of a “culture of corruption” that extends from 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue in Washington to the edges of Central Park in New York. Others imply it is part of a different pattern: the purchase of more and more of America’s most valuable assets by companies and sovereign wealth funds from the Persian Gulf’s petrostates, at times orchestrated by those in and around the second Trump administration. Those shareholders wonder whether Lutnick had personally worked behind the scenes to maneuver the Khashoggi group into place to buy the Pierre, and that speculation spilled onto the pages of The New York Times.

BALL GAMES Guests attend a Valentino party in the Cotillion Ballroom at the Pierre hotel, 1970, New York.

In a recent development, A source close to Lutnick notes that he formally cut ties with Newmark in early 2025 and adds that, since his move to government, Lutnick’s only involvement in the Pierre sales process has been to respond to media reports like this one. A spokesperson for Sabre Park Avenue LLC, Khashoggi’s American holding company, tells Vanity Fair in a statement that “any insinuation or implication that the proposal, the transaction or the parties involved engaged in improper or undisclosed conduct is categorically false.”.

I spoke to more than 15 sources and reviewed hundreds of pages of documents related to the Pierre deal, including previously unreported text messages between Lutnick and Khashoggi and a corporate intelligence dossier dropped in my mailbox.

Turns out, the shareholders were right to wonder about Lutnick’s role.

In a recent development, the Pierre for decades was synonymous with New York glamour. At the height of their star power, Audrey Hepburn stayed in the hotel’s suites and Elizabeth Taylor kept an apartment there. The restaurant’s original menu was created by Escoffier. Barbara Walters had a reception for her final wedding at the Pierre (about 10 years after she and my grandfather, the Broadway producer Lee Guber, officially split). Yves Saint Laurent owned a two-bedroom on the 38th floor, which was later bought by Valentino cofounder Giancarlo Giammetti, who then sold it to former Bottega Veneta creative director Tomas Maier.

Industry observers note that and yet for 15 years or more, there’s been a growing sense that the Pierre’s best days are behind it, even as the stars continue to use the hotel to get ready for the Met Gala. A 2010 Wall Street Journal article mentions how the Pierre “lost its glory.” By the time Lutnick swooped in to buy the penthouse in 2017, he did so at an $81 million discount off its original asking price.

THE TORY PARTY Fashion designer Tory Burch, in one of the hotel’s elevators, was among the residents opposed to the sale.

Since then, age has continued to take its toll. Scaffolding has surrounded the hotel since at least 2018, according to city records. Exit a multimillion-dollar apartment with a spectacular view of the park and you’re liable to find worn carpets or hallways with the faint odor of mold. Rooms at the Pierre tend to cost much less than they do at the Plaza or the Ritz-Carlton, just around the corner.

Over time, a group of shareholders became particularly vexed with Taj Hotels, which had managed the property since 2005. There were complaints of broken elevators, empty concierge desks, and “slipshod maintenance.” Maier, in an October 2023 co-op-wide email, lamented that Taj delayed long-planned renovations to his apartment for months, citing high hotel occupancy. (A Taj spokesperson stated in a statement those concerns “reflected a specific point in time rather than the overall trajectory of the property.”).

Recent findings suggest that what Maier may not have known—and what the residents I spoke to were unaware of—was that the Pierre’s board had already explored the possibility of replacing Taj. The only way to do that, to break the contract with Taj, was to sell the Pierre. In April 2023, the board drafted a memorandum of understanding with the Maybourne Hotel Group, which is primarily owned by members of the Qatari royal family, to buy the hotel portion of the Pierre. “But there was a condition,” a source familiar with the matter tells me. “Everybody had to move out for two years.” The source adds, “You cannot renovate a 100-year-old building with people living in it, right?”.

In a recent development, that was a deal killer. So the board decided, in this source’s words, to hire a firm that could broker a “more acceptable” sale. They picked the real estate consultancy Newmark. Lutnick was still chairman of Newmark’s board at that time, though two sources say he had no role in the decision. (The board, through its attorney, declined to comment for this story. But a Newmark spokesperson says its “unanimous” selection was “based on the firm’s experience advising on some of New York City’s most complex and high-profile real estate transactions.”).

Industry observers note that from there, “Newmark went out to find another buyer,” the first source adds. Its fee at the time: $50,000 per month, to be counted against any future commissions in the event of a sale. (Eventually that was bargained down to a flat $30 million.) The board retained the high-profile law firm Fried Frank, which had represented Lutnick’s companies before, to assist Newmark in its search.

LONDON'S CALLING Christopher Cowdray, the Dorchester Collection’s president, was part of the contentious presentation to residents in the Cotillion ballroom at the Pierre.

Since Lutnick’s financial firm, Cantor Fitzgerald, owned a controlling stake in Newmark, that gave Lutnick an incentive to see the Pierre sold. He had another: According to the source connected to Lutnick, his 12,000-square-foot penthouse triplex had been uninhabitable since 2021, when a storm had caused catastrophic damage. Lutnick concluded, according to the source close to him, that major repairs wouldn’t make sense if they weren’t accompanied by a larger round of structural renovations to the building. In the meantime, he installed a basketball court in the apartment to make some use of the place.

In a recent development, when the sales process started, the idea was to make a deal for the hotel only. The new owner would likely want to consolidate guest rooms on certain floors. That meant some Pierre residents might be encouraged—strongly encouraged—to sell, but not necessarily everyone.

Brokers approached everyone from Mark Zuckerberg to Michael Dell to the king of Morocco to buy the place. Most of the residents were in the dark. As far as they knew, Newmark was trying to help renovate the building, not sell it off. Nor did they know Lutnick was personally trying to wrangle potential buyers for the Pierre.

According to recent reports, on Wednesday, May 8, 2024, Lutnick’s private jet took off from Teterboro, Latest Jersey, outside of New York. Lutnick was on his way to Paris to meet with the Arnault family who, as part of their dominion over LVMH, run the Cheval Blanc hotel group. The source close to Lutnick mentions he had long admired the hotels and pitched the idea of the Pierre joining the group.

It has been revealed that lutnick’s first stop, however, was in London. After his plane landed, he went to the Dorchester Collection’s eponymous hotel in Mayfair. Shortly after 9 a.m. on Thursday, Lutnick gathered with Cowdray, the Dorchester president, and Motasem Khashoggi, chairman and principal owner of the Khashoggi Holding Company. From the outside, it seemed like an unlikely trio. The Khashoggi family was mainly famous for its wealth, but that was decades ago, back when Adnan, Motasem’s relative, was one of the world’s leading arms dealers. Motasem is recognized internationally today not as a captain of Saudi industry but as the primary legal representative for the Khashoggi family following the brutal 2018 murder of his journalist cousin, Jamal, by the Saudi state.

The source close to Lutnick states he and Khashoggi “met and spoke about a variety of different things” in London, “including: Wouldn’t it be cool if the Pierre was a Dorchester Collection hotel.” Eight days after the London meeting, according to screenshots of WhatsApp messages reviewed by Vanity Fair, Khashoggi texted Lutnick to say that “Brunie”—Hassanal Bolkiah, the Sultan of Brunei, who owns the Dorchester Collection—had “directly” asked him to explore a deal for the Pierre.

Khashoggi then asked Lutnick if he could give one of his kids a summer internship and provided his phone number. (Vanity Fair verified that number, as well as the ones used by Lutnick and the elder Khashoggi in the chats.) Lutnick quickly agreed to the father’s request. “We would be delighted to have your son join us,” he wrote. “I’m excited to invest in and build exciting companies together.”.

A week later, Khashoggi sent the chat his greetings “from rainy Frankfurt,” along with a draft letter of intent to the Pierre’s board to begin due diligence for a “potential acquisition of The Pierre Hotel” and a initiative to buy up “the remaining residential units.”.

Lutnick wrote back on Memorial Day. “I am flying to Europe this evening, Italy and France,” he texted. “I’ve made a few modifications to the letter of intent.” Promise a “complete renovation of the guest rooms, public areas, dining facilities, and amenities,” Lutnick suggested. And be sure to include target prices, both per room and for the whole thing.

Recent findings suggest that lutnick’s firm, Newmark, was supposed to be representing the sellers in this transaction. Yet here Lutnick was coaching potential buyers, in effect putting himself on both sides of the deal. It wasn’t a cardinal sin in the take-no-prisoners worlds of Upcoming York City real estate or MAGA politics, but it wasn’t strictly kosher either.

Recent findings suggest that lutnick was confirmed as commerce secretary in February 2025; he stepped down from his Newmark chairmanship then and transferred his Cantor Fitzgerald assets to his sons. Lutnick was still listed as a member of the Pierre’s “transaction committee” in March, when the board confirmed in a letter that Newmark was in negotiations with an unnamed “operator.” But not to worry, the board added: “No owner would be required to sell their unit or move to another one.”.

Sources indicate that residents scrambled to find out more. All they got back were rumors and whispers. One shareholder’s representative says he heard the chatter but “blew it off,” thinking that nervous residents were being “dramatic.” According to this representative, the attorneys at Holland & Knight, which had represented the Pierre for years, seemed to be in the dark as well. “You can’t sell a co-op. Never happening here,” one of those lawyers told the representative in this source’s recounting. (Holland & Knight declined to comment for this story.).

In a recent development, in June 2025, the New York Post reported that the Sultan of Brunei was in talks to buy the Pierre, along with Essam ­Khashoggi, an older relative of Motasem’s. The board, chaired by Michael Stern, didn’t provide many specifics in a July Zoom with shareholders but emphasized that a sale was in their best interest, according to multiple published accounts. Two months later, according to court filings, four co-op board members—the investor John Levin, former Coca-Cola CEO Douglas Daft, the lawyer and movie producer David G. Johnson, and former KB Home chief executive Bruce Karatz—approved a nonbinding term sheet to sell the Pierre.

Sources indicate that on September 16, at a gathering in the Cotillion Ballroom, Fried Frank lawyers broke the news to shareholders. Khashoggi Holding was the buyer, and the sultan’s Dorchester Collection would be the hotel’s managers. The price was astronomical, they stated, and would guarantee residents “at least three times the market value” for their apartments, Town & Country reported. But the transaction was different from the one discussed back in March. It was not just for the hotel and selected apartments. It was for the whole building, which meant the co-op owners had to vacate within 12 months. All of them.

BREAKFAST NEAR TIFFANY'S A young woman enjoys room service at the Pierre Hotel, 1943.

It has been revealed that an escrow account of $10 million, funded by the shareholders, would be “used for eviction proceedings” for any residents who refused to leave, according to a slideshow presentation delivered by the lawyers that day. And on that happy note, residents were encouraged to open the personalized envelopes that had been given to them at the door, one for each shareholder. Inside were estimates of how much they might get from a sale.

It has been revealed that one person who was there says it reminded him of a “game show,” and kind of an insulting one to the ultrarich in the room, for whom a few million dollars either way wouldn’t matter all that much. What was particularly galling, according to sources at the meeting, was the plan for the building’s union employees. Many of them, they noted, were like family—to each other and to the residents. The staff would have to begin to go even sooner. Before Khashoggi would be asked to put down a penny, Fried Frank noted in its presentation, the firm “will engage with the Hotel Gaming and Trades Union to negotiate terms for the termination of the Union Contract.”.

Sources indicate that employees at the Pierre tend to talk about their tenures in decades. “I only have 12 years here,” one staffer tells me without irony. Some ­workers have jobs that are so old-school, they’re not really jobs anywhere else: elevator drivers, telephone switchboard operators. Housekeeping staff wear black-and-white outfits that wouldn’t have been out of place in Audrey Hepburn’s day. “I’m very used to it,” this employee says, referring to the atmosphere at the Pierre. She means that as a positive.

Like many Pierre staffers, she’s an immigrant. A 2021 New Yorker profile counted “49 languages” spoken by the staff, “including Cantonese, Creole, Danish, Farsi, Greek, Hindi, Japanese, Portuguese, Russian, Tagalog, Tamil, Tibetan, and Twi.” I spoke with employees who are originally from four different continents.

Industry observers note that one was a man I’ll call Ray, who has put in more than a quarter century at the Pierre and would very much like to keep going, even if the severance deal written into his union contract is pretty sweet: Ray figures he could live off of it for a year. But then what? He’s still got kids in school. And at the other hotels in town, the competition for open positions is really intense; promotions come mostly from within. “The chances of getting hired [in his particular department] are almost zero,” Ray tells me. “So I wouldn’t want to get a buyout. I don’t want the hotel to be closed.” Just in case, he’s taken a part-time gig elsewhere.

Industry observers note that “We’re not like these millionaires, billionaires, the Howard Lutnicks, the Tory Burches,” states another Pierre employee. “Just working people, trying to protect their families.”.

The rumors about a sale have been around long enough, and loud enough, that they rattled the staffers I spoke to. Even a renovation could upend staffers’ lives: The remodeling at the Waldorf Astoria Hotel lasted eight years; more than 1,200 union workers were bought out of their contracts. “Most of us, we worry,” a housekeeper tells me.

People move to the Pierre, in part, because of the staff. More than a few residents come to be taken care of, to be treated like five-star hotel guests in their own (second, or third) homes. Room service is available from 6:45 a.m. to 10:45 p.m. Housekeeping comes in seven days a week; the apartments I saw were immaculate in every way, part of the reason why maintenance costs can run tens of thousands of dollars per month. (“I haven’t made a bed since I was a kid,” states one long-term resident.).

It has been revealed that my mom for years talked about retiring to a place like this, not that she could’ve afforded it. For older people who can, it’s a way to have the help they need while still living on their own. You see a lot of women who’ve lost or split up with their rich husbands: Beriro, the philanthropist and animal-rights activist; Gale Hayman, the cofounder of Giorgio’s of Beverly Hills; Mimi Sternlicht, the social entrepreneur; Julie Opperman, the prolific author whose late husband started the Westlaw legal-research service.

It has been revealed that you could, perhaps, confuse these women for pushovers, one Belle Vivier pump away from assisted living. At the July meeting, Dorchester and Khashoggi brought gifts for the shareholders: bright-red teddy bears. “For little old ladies to snuggle up to in their beds,” one resident laughs at lunch afterward. Then she grabbed my utensils to cut my food.

These ladies were long past cuddly tchotchkes. Over time, several residents, most of them women and most of them over 65, had formed a loose coalition to learn what they could about the deal for the Pierre and figure ways to stop it. “It was a handful of older women,” the resident adds, “banging on the pipes, saying, ‘Listen up, people!’ ”.

Some of them, at least at first, were open to the idea of a sale; they had other homes, after all. But the cloak of secrecy around the deal infuriated them. So in the days leading up to the contentious reveal of the Khashoggi proposal in September 2025, Chiles and Beriro and others banded together with Hearst and Burch—relative youngsters—and lawyered up. “We became an informal little group: Tory and a bunch of widows,” one source with direct knowledge of the matter says, tongue a bit in cheek.

ABOVE BOARD Investor Austin Hearst is part of a group of Pierre residents who sued the co-op board to produce more information about the sale of the building.

It has been revealed that in November 2025, the group sued the board to force it to produce more information about the sale, with Burch’s LLC as the lead plaintiff: how much the board really knew about the buyer; which third parties might benefit from it. Shortly after, Fried Frank lawyer Michael Keats criticized Burch in a letter to her attorney: “this [her tactics] comes across as completely unhinged.” On at least one occasion, according to a source familiar with the matter, a board member approached Burch to see if she might want to keep her apartment, even while Khashoggi bought everyone else’s. Burch refused. (“The Board never offered anyone any special consideration,” its president and chairman later wrote in a letter to shareholders.).

The suit was quickly dismissed when the board agreed to release some of the information.

Sources indicate that A number of shareholders, meanwhile, had found other sources. Some of them enlisted, in the resident’s words, “spies” to ferret out what the sale truly entailed. In March, some shareholders, independently of the board, met with Taj CEO Puneet Chhatwal. People both for and against the deal pressed shareholders for how they were going to vote, like Capitol Hill whips.

In late July, a 41-page corporate intelligence dossier was delivered to my home in an unmarked envelope. Who commissioned it is unclear; the cover page is missing and the report is undated. But it provides a tough assessment of Khashoggi’s corporate expertise.

According to the report, none of Khashoggi Holding’s “eight subsidiaries and associated companies” operate in the “hospitality sector, and none appear to have any international presence or cross-border real estate capability.”.

The company’s “most prominent publicly reported investments to date,” it adds, are an approximately $37 million “pharmaceutical investment in Aleppo [Syria] and a cement factory partnership.” Other deals publicly linked to the company and to Motasem Khashoggi are substantial but of a similar size.

In recent years and especially in the second Trump administration, money from the Persian Gulf has backed an attempt to merge two of America’s iconic movie studios, completed a leveraged buyout of one of its biggest video game makers, and purchased some of Newly introduced York’s most prized office towers. Khashoggi’s deals, on the other hand, “are orders of magnitude smaller than the proposed Pierre Hotel acquisition,” notes the report, which claims that the tech giant’s “registered capital” amounts to “approximately USD 266,000.”.

Perhaps it’s just a coincidence that during the July meeting in the Cotillion Ballroom, the Khashoggi and Dorchester representatives received question after question about how Motasem Khashoggi could possibly have the resources to buy the Pierre.

Recent findings suggest that NEIGHBOR VS. NEIGHBOR Michael Eisner, the former Disney CEO, owns two apartments in the Pierre. He has been in favor of finding latest ownership for the hotel.

“You mentioned the Khashoggi LLC is the buyer, but who is putting up the money behind the Khashoggi hedge fund?” one shareholder asked.

“There is no hedge fund. This is Mr. Khashoggi. This will be funded in all cash, and it is only him,” was the answer.

“We’re not going to leave you out there with an unfunded buyer,” added Patrick Dowd, a Fried Frank lawyer.

Industry observers note that the questions would prove prescient—but it would still be a couple of months before that became clear. In the meantime, the speculation and the finger-pointing continued—splitting neighbor from neighbor—as the possibility of a sale grew closer and residents had taken sides. “They run the hotel, in my opinion, very badly,” Eisner noted of Taj in that July Cotillion room meeting, adding that he “would not stay at this hotel” with them in charge.

“Then sell your apartment. If you’re not happy here, leave,” Burch snapped, according to the same recording of the meeting. “You don’t have to force everyone else and fire 700 employees in the process.”.

“This is not your home,” Burch remarked a moment later to a second shareholder, who tried to take Eisner’s side. The decay, the imperfections, they can be a hassle, for sure. But they’re also part of the throwback charm, a necessary side effect to living someplace with so much history. “I don’t need a shiny latest hotel,” she added. “People actually love this place, as shabby as it may be.”.

Despite the rancor, the board and the Indian hotel operators tried to negotiate a way forward. Or at least a competitive offer to Khashoggi’s. After 10 months of talks, they finally came to what they thought was an agreement. Two agreements, actually: one to buy the hotel portion of the Pierre; the other to extend Taj’s lease, in exchange for a commitment to invest almost $400 million into the building. The idea was to give both options to shareholders, shortly after the Khashoggi presentation.

Sources indicate that then suddenly, with less than a week to go before the Cotillion room meeting, Taj withdrew. The bosses in Mumbai voted not to approve the transactions they had been negotiating.

GLOVES OFF Al Pacino’s blind tango in Scent of a Woman takes place the Pierre's Cotillion ballroom.

Sources indicate that A letter from Chhatwal floating the idea of a $300 million investment was rejected out of hand by the co-op board. The heads of the board wrote to shareholders the next day: It’s Khashoggi or the status quo, no other choices.

“Do you want to live here or do you not? Let’s not overcomplicate it,” Burch told the Cotillion room. “It’s going to be down to two options. You either stay with Taj. Or you leave, and then it becomes some fancy hotel that we have nothing to do with.”.

Recent findings suggest that about a month later, the board released the details of the Khashoggi deal in a proxy statement sent to residents. It was enormous—more than 200 pages—but perhaps not maximally persuasive. Departing residents were promised five free nights in a suite at one of Dorchester’s other high-end hotels, plus a set of perks. “Priority access to spa treatments” and free breakfast seemed unlikely to move the needle with a crowd accustomed to more elaborate pampering.

Sources indicate that the following week, Khashoggi tried reaching out to shareholders directly. “I understand how personal this is,” he wrote. “I sincerely hope that you will welcome me and my family into the Pierre family.”.

This personal appeal did not work on those shareholders who were already dug in against the deal. “Where do you get off addressing me by my first name?” one emailed back to Khashoggi.

And with that, the window opened for voting the deal up or down.

The following day, the chairman and president of the Pierre’s co-op board wrote to residents that “a wire transfer instruction has been issued to transmit the $100,000,000 deposit.”.

Then something strange happened. Or rather, didn’t happen at all.

Khashoggi’s money didn’t show up.

Supporters of the sale were baffled. “We are told by all advisers involved that he’s, you know, intending to complete the transaction,” one of those supporters says. “In my business experience, someone who is a wealthy individual who decides that they don’t want to do the deal,” this person adds, “they send you a nice letter or make a phone call and say, you know, ‘I’m very sorry, but circumstances have changed, and I’m moving on.’ ”.

In a recent development, that call never came, though. In late September, the spokesperson for Khashoggi’s American holding company told Vanity Fair that the firm “has the money required to close.”.

Sources indicate that the board gave Khashoggi additional time to come up with the deposit. He failed to do so, and the sale was called off. All of that work, all of those millions spent, all of that rancor—turned out, it was for a lost cause. The Khashoggi deal was dead.

In an interview with the Times, Khashoggi gave a dog-ate-my-homework excuse, blaming the bank for failing to send over his deposit. He gave a shout-out to his “good friend” Lutnick, who had led him to the Pierre deal in the first place and who had been poised to receive as much as a $100 million windfall from it. Then Khashoggi took a shot at the residents he was courting just a few weeks earlier. “They have their building, which I’m sure they know the condition of,” he said. “And I have my money. So I don’t know who’s the bigger loser here.”.

Industry observers note that at the time of publication, an election for a new co-op board was set for December 1. At least one of the residents who opposed the Khashoggi sale is mulling a run; another of those shareholders is thinking about suing those folks who got them into this whole mess.

Recent findings suggest that but in theory, things at the Pierre will now largely go back to the way they were. Or at least they’ll continue along the same trajectory. Taj has more than 8 years left on its lease, plus an option to extend another 10. Together with the new board, they’ll figure out which of the renovations are a priority. Those costs will then be split with residents. The assessments could reach into the millions for each apartment. The disruptions from the construction could be considerable. No one will be forced to leave their homes in this crumbling old palace by the park. For now, the elevator drivers and switchboard operators get to stay.

  • Unfortunately, creator Quinn Shephard and co-showrunner Gina Gammell didn't tell Glamour all the biggest secrets surrounding Grace and whether this is truly spiritual or classic Catholic School drama, Luckily, though, fans did learn a couple of key details.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Netflix's The Body was one of the unexpected hits of the 2026 TV schedule. While it's still yet to be confirmed whether we'll get to stream a second season with a Netflix subscription, it feels like the odds are looking good. So I'm glad the executive producers/showrunners are already shooting down some fan theories before any newly introduced episodes come out.

Unfortunately, creator Quinn Shephard and co-showrunner Gina Gammell didn't tell Glamour all the biggest secrets surrounding Grace and whether this is truly spiritual or classic Catholic School drama, Luckily, though, fans did learn a couple of key details. I'm happy about both of these theories being addressed, especially the one that sounds like good news for Leo.

Industry observers note that if you're a fan of Leo and think he's too pure for this world, Quinn Shepard confirming he did not bring a snake to the Halloween party should bring you some comfort. It's been theorized that Leo brought his pet snake to the party, perhaps in an attempt to heal Grace. This was supported by the fact that Leo and Grace came from a cult called Signs Following, which used snake handling as a means of showing the faith of its followers.

Recent findings suggest that additionally, Leo seemed concerned about other characters outside of his family seeing the snake during the investigation into Grace's coma. With this context, it's possible that Leo was just concerned about hiding their true religious beliefs, as they lied about being Catholics to get rehomed after leaving West Virginia.

I'm so glad the EPs have also confirmed the Lions won't be going to jail after what happened to Grace. I thought that was a possibility, given Anya's confession and the various details about the party that came out toward the end of Season 1.

I Just Watched The Trailer For Netflix's JonBenèt Ramsey Drama, And I Feel A Bit Uneasy.

In a recent development, while I'm all for accountability in teen dramas, especially when it comes to Riverdale's Archie Andrews, I'll let it slide for The Body. Sending Anya or any of the Lions to jail or prison for their actions at the party would've created a major genre shift in the story, and I'm far more interested in the story remaining around the school after Season 1's ending.

In a recent development, of course, we still have to wait for official word on Season 2 of The Body. While I think Netflix should be bullish on a renewal given the talented young cast and the fact it's been on Netflix's Top 10 charts in recent weeks, there's really no telling what the streamer will decide to do with the series. It's a well known fact that the company has canceled plenty of shows way too soon, so we best just cross our fingers and hope a Grace-sized miracle grants the series a renewal soon.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

Recent findings suggest that as mentioned, The Body is available to stream, and there are other upcoming Netflix shows that will be worth checking out as well. With the holidays approaching, now is the time to catch up on everything you missed this year, and there's so much to enjoy!

The Further Mis-Adventures Of Cliff Booth Features A Delightful Quentin Tarantino Easter Egg

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (409 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Spoilers for "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" follow.
  • Real ones know that Quentin Tarantino has been building his own cinematic universe for years.
  • According to recent reports, tarantino didn't direct "Cliff Booth" — he handed those duties over to David Fincher.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Spoilers for "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" follow.

Forget the MCU. Real ones know that Quentin Tarantino has been building his own cinematic universe for years. For instance: while this is never officially stated by anyone on screen, Michael Madsen's character from "Reservoir Dogs" is supposed to be the brother of John Travolta's character from "Pulp Fiction" (there was even a proposal for a crossover movie, but it never happened). Beyond character connections, Tarantino also likes to drop his own fictional products into his films, and "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" keeps this trend going.

According to recent reports, tarantino didn't direct "Cliff Booth" — he handed those duties over to David Fincher. But Tarantino still wrote the script, and Fincher keeps the Easter eggs intact. The biggest example: Substantial Kahuna Burger. Early in the film, we see Brad Pitt's Cliff Booth pick up some food at Big Kahuna Burger to bring home to his dad, Gus (Peter Weller). Tarantino fans will, of course, recognize that burger joint: it was prominently mentioned in "Pulp Fiction," and we see Samuel L. Jackson's character Jules take a big bite of a burger while intimidating some crooks who are about to meet a violent end.

Sources indicate that but wait, there's more! Another Tarantino product that reveals up in "The Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" are the famous Red Apple Cigarettes. Red Apples have been mentioned in virtually every Tarantino film, and they were even a part of "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood," the film that "Cliff Booth" serves as a sequel to.

According to recent reports, in "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood," Leonardo DiCaprio's Rick Dalton filmed a commercial for Red Apple Cigarettes (believe it or not, kids, there used to be commercials for cigarettes on TV). "The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth" keeps the tradition alive while also giving us a nice little callback. During one scene, we see Cliff watching a new Red Apple commercial on TV. And who is starring in that commercial? None other than Sharon Tate, played by Margot Robbie in a cameo.

Sources indicate that "Once Upon a Time in Hollywood" ended by literally changing history, and allowing Sharon Tate and her friends to completely avoid their tragic murders at the hands of the Manson family. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Aaron Rodgers is one of the best-ever quarterbacks to play in the NFL, but it’s often his antics off the field that get the most people talking.

Rodgers — who was the Green Bay Packers superstar quarterback for 18 seasons before joining the Latest York Jets in 2023 and the Pittsburgh Steelers in 2025 — came under fire in November 2021 when it was revealed he misled people about his COVID-19 vaccination status when he told reporters that he was “immunized” when he hadn’t actually been vaccinated.

The athlete defended his use of the phrase, calling it “the truth.”.

According to recent reports, “Had there been a follow-up to my statement that I’d been immunized, I would have responded with this: I would have said, ‘Look, I’m not some sort of anti-vax-flat-Earther. I’m somebody who’s a critical thinker,’” Rodgers later explained on the Pat McAfee Show. “I march to the beat of my own drum. I believe strongly in bodily autonomy, [in the] ability to make choices for your body, not to have to acquiesce to some woke culture or crazed group of individuals who say you have to do something.”.

He raised eyebrows again in November 2026, when his controversial comments about Steelers head coach Mike McCarthy amid his benching ended with the team releasing the quarterback hours later.

Keep scrolling for all of Rodgers’ controversies through the years:.

While a contestant on The Bachelorette in 2016, Aaron’s brother Jordan Rodgers told future wife JoJo Fletcher that he and Aaron “don’t really have that much of a relationship.”.

“It’s just kind of the way he’s chosen to do life and I’ve chosen to stay close with my family and my parents and my brother,” Jordan explained at the time. “Yeah, it’s not ideal and I love him and I can’t imagine what it’s like to be in his shoes and have the pressure he has, the demands from people that he has. Don’t have hard feelings against him, it’s just how things go right now.”.

The brothers’ estrangement only grew worse as the years went on, particularly after both Jordan and other brother Luke Rodgers called out Aaron for allegedly not being there for their family amid the California wildfires in 2018. (Aaron also missed Jordan’s wedding in 2022.).

In Aaron’s 2024 Netflix docuseries, Aaron Rodgers: Enigma, he reflected on the strain Jordan’s Bachelorette stint put on their relationship.

“It wasn’t like I was super duper close with everybody in the family. I was close with my little brother [Jordan],” Aaron said. “But in actuality, it goes back to stuff from high school that kind of made me feel distant. Stuff in college, stuff post-college. I was quiet about it. I thought the best way to do it was just don’t talk about it publicly.”.

He recalled that Jordan — and the show producers — did the opposite of that by making it clear during hometowns that Aaron was absent. “And what do they do? They go on a bulls— show and leave two empty chairs,” Aaron mentioned. “They all agreed this was a good thing to do, to leave two empty chairs at a stupid dating show that my brother just went on to get famous — his words, not mine. That he ended up winning. But a dinner that was during the season, I was never asked to go to. Not that I would’ve gone.”.

Recent findings suggest that aaron also alleged in the December 2024 doc that he “found a lot of resistance” from his family when he stopped practicing the same Christian religion he was taught as a child. Instead, the athlete turned to “other religions and plant medicine” which fueled his “alternative lifestyle.” The religious shift “definitely changed the dynamics of my family,” he added.

In November 2026, Aaron and Jordan reunited and shared photo of their hangout. The pair’s reunion came after Aaron and Luke were spotted together on the sidelines at a Steelers game.

It has been revealed that aaron — who contracted COVID-19 in November 2021 — was forced to pay $14,650 for breaking NFL COVID-19 safety protocols as an unvaccinated player. His violations included attending a party with other teammates and speaking to reporters without a mask on. The Packers were fined $300,000 for not disciplining him or reporting his violations.

In August 2022, Aaron claimed on “The Aubrey Marcus Podcast” that doing ayahuasca helped him win two back-to-back MVP awards in 2020 and 2021.

Sources indicate that “I don’t think it’s a coincidence. I really don’t. I don’t really believe in coincidences at this point,” he said. “It’s the universe bringing things to happen when they’re supposed to happen and there’s signs and synchronicities all around us at all times if we’re awake enough to see them and to take them in and to listen to our intuition when it’s speaking to us or, you know, pounding us in the head saying, ‘Hey dummy, this is what you’re supposed to be doing.'”.

In November 2022, Packers backup QB DeShone Kizer claimed on “The Breneman Show” podcast that Aaron once encouraged him to question whether the September 11 attacks happened.

“He shut the door, and the first thing that comes out of Aaron Rodgers’ mouth was ‘Do you believe in 9/11?’” Kizer recalled, noting that Aaron wanted him to “‘read up on that’” and to “go back and look into some of the conspiracies around it.”.

In a recent development, during multiple off-seasons, Aaron kept fans — and the Green Bay Packers — waiting for long periods of time while he publicly hinted at a possible desire to be traded or retire altogether. After ultimately sticking with the Packers every time, in 2023 he and the team finally pulled the trigger when Aaron was traded to the Jets.

Buffalo Bills QB Josh Allen called out Aaron for allegedly cheating at the AT&T Pebble Beach Pro-Am golf tournament in February 2023.

It has been revealed that “I love Aaron, but he did [cheat],” Allen stated on Barstool Sports’ “Pardon My Take” podcast in August 2023. Allen accused Aaron of “sandbagging,” meaning he downplayed how good he was at golf before the match in order to be afforded extra strokes during the match.

According to recent reports, “He may have gotten seven or eight strokes too many at Pebble Beach, or nine,” Allen claimed “other sources” remarked. Then he joked, “I think Aaron Rodgers should be in jail.”.

It has been revealed that jimmy Kimmel found himself in a years-long feud with Aaron after he poked fun at the NFL star’s controversial COVID-19 vaccine beliefs in 2021. “Nothing says I heal myself with crystals like this haircut — that little knot on top,” Kimmel said in a November 2021 Jimmy Kimmel Live! monologue before flashing to a selfie of Rodgers in a man bun. “Aaron is a Karen, that’s the fact of the matter.”.

According to recent reports, in March 2023, Aaron revealed on The Pat McAfee Show that he was interested in seeing the list of names that were connected to the late convicted sex trafficker Jeffrey Epstein. Kimmel shared snippets of Aaron’s interview on his show and implied that he might have a potential head injury.

Sources indicate that aaron didn’t respond at the time, but he stoked the fire in January 2024 when he insinuated that Kimmel should be worried about the names on Epstein’s list coming out — implying that the comedian had some connection to the accused sex offender. “I’ll tell you what, if that list comes out, I will definitely be popping some sort of bottle,” Aaron said on The Pat McAfee Show.

Kimmel slammed Aaron via X for his remarks, denying any connection to Epstein. “Dear A——-: for the record, I’ve not met, flown with, visited, or had any contact whatsoever with Epstein, nor will you find my name on any ‘list’ other than the clearly-phony nonsense that soft-brained wackos like yourself can’t seem to distinguish from reality,” Kimmel wrote in January 2024. “Your reckless words put my family in danger. Keep it up and we will debate the facts further in court. @AaronRodgers12.”.

After Kimmel went off on Aaron’s reckless accusations and actions on his talk show, the quarterback responded to the backlash. “I wish him the best. I don’t give a s— what he indicates about me,” Aaron noted on a January 2024 episode of The Pat McAfee Show. “As long as he understands what I actually said, that I’m not accusing him of being on a list. I’m all for moving forward.”.

Aaron raised eyebrows in September 2024 when he was caught pushing Jets coach Robert Saleh away when he came in for a hug during their game against the Fresh England Patriots. The awkward moment caused some viewers to think there was tension between the player and coach.

It has been revealed that “He’s not a big hugger usually,” Aaron remarked of Saleh in his postgame press conference, explaining, “So I didn’t know he was going for the hug. He likes to do the two-hand chest push.” He insisted the moment “wasn’t awkward at all,” which Saleh echoed himself.

Industry observers note that the following month, amid the Jets disappointing start to the season, Saleh was fired. Rumors began to swirl that Aaron’s relationship with Saleh played into the franchise’s choice to let him go, which he denied. “As far as any of the ridiculous allegations out there, I’m not going to spend more than one sentence in response to it,” Aaron noted during an October 2024 appearance on The Pat McAfee Show. “I resent any of those accusations because they’re patently false.”.

During his first day at the Pittsburgh Steelers’ training camp in June 2025, Rodgers shared that he had gotten married “a couple months” earlier. The quarterback did not reveal the identity of his spouse. However, he revealed in December 2024 that he was dating a woman named Brittani.

In November 2026, news broke that the Steelers were benching Aaron ahead of the team’s Thanksgiving week game against the Denver Broncos after back-to-back losses. Following the shocking decision, Aaron appeared on The Pat McAfee Show and aired his grievances with head coach McCarthy.

Aaron accused McCarthy of sleeping through meetings, missing a walkthrough and being “unhealthy.” He also claimed that McCarthy yelled, “One, two, three, Packers!” during a huddle break, hinting that he was unaware of which team he was actually coaching.

#120140. Are the World’s Top Literary Scholars Being Targeted by a Chinese Spy Op?

Are the World’s Top Literary Scholars Being Targeted by a Chinese Spy Op?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2929 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vanityfair

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stephanie Newell, an English professor at Yale University, was thrilled when she got the email inviting her to be an honorary fellow at the International Institute of Literature & Arts.
  • The letter, signed by one Julian Lee “on behalf of the Secretariat” of IILA, invited Newell to join highly esteemed literature scholars at the Ivies, Stanford, Oxford, and Cambridge.
  • This one, it seemed, came without strings.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stephanie Newell, an English professor at Yale University, was thrilled when she got the email inviting her to be an honorary fellow at the International Institute of Literature & Arts. She had never heard of IILA, but she recognized several prestigious names of fellow big-time literature professors who were listed among its fellows. “I saw Gayatri Spivak and Homi Bhabha, Franco Moretti, and I was like, Oh, finally,” she says.

The letter, signed by one Julian Lee “on behalf of the Secretariat” of IILA, invited Newell to join highly esteemed literature scholars at the Ivies, Stanford, Oxford, and Cambridge. Newell, who has taught world and African literature at Yale for more than a decade, had been inducted into other prestigious societies with many of these same scholars, such as the British Academy.

This one, it seemed, came without strings. “There are no fees or membership dues,” read the letter. “Participation in award reviews, academic meetings, and consultation will be arranged with you in advance and subject to your availability.”.

Stephanie Newell, an English professor at Yale University, was initially honored to receive an IILA fellowship.

In a recent development, it seemed like a no-brainer. They’d also given her an award, and she even decided to accept an offer to join IILA’s academic committee. Yale was pleased for her too. The English department posted an announcement congratulating her on receiving the award.

Then she started to see red flags.

Soon, Newell says, she was listed among IILA’s leadership, even though she’d only agreed to be a committee member. “Please will you remove my name,” she wrote in an email to Lee.

Sources indicate that her concerns compounded when she received a draft of IILA’s bulletin, featuring a perplexingly poorly written biography—not what one would expect from a fancy literary academy. “Please delete my profile from the Bulletin,” Newell asked Lee, “as it contains too many errors for circulation, and is very poorly written.”.

It has been revealed that while the institute’s membership ranks included many of Newell’s high-profile peers, there were also a number of names on the list that seemed a bit random. Pat Barker, a novelist rather than a scholar, seemed out of place among the critics and theorists. There were, however, about half a dozen Chinese professors (including one who had already died).

“I’ve always been a bit of a doubting Thomas,” Newell wrote in an email to a colleague on the list who confirmed that she, too, had accepted the fellowship despite not knowing who was behind it. “I’m starting to wonder what’s going on and whether we’ve been somehow flattered into something that doesn’t exist!” Newell wrote.

That’s when Newell, who was my professor when I was a Yale undergraduate, decided to reach out to me about “a fake academic institute that has sucked in numerous very high-profile professors.” This was a couple of weeks ago, right after the news broke of Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman US authorities believed to be a Chinese spy. It made sense what China would want from Huang, the CEO of the powerful AI chip maker Nvidia, but could world literature professors really be a target? I started digging, which led me down a rabbit hole that included an entire constellation of shadow academies that former national security officials say have real potential to be part of a Chinese intelligence operation.

Sources indicate that the website for IILA, which claims to be based in California, appears to have been registered in China. An IT specialist who reviewed the website for Vanity Fair assessed that it was built using artificial intelligence and riddled with glitches and broken links. The file name of the site’s logo is the Chinese word for “picture.” Registration records list the owner’s location as the Hubei province in central China, whose capital is Wuhan. But a data bug in the site’s administrative code suggests that the computer being used to post news on the site is not in China, but likely in Southeast Asia. The bug leaks the computer’s time zone with every new post saved through the site’s form, and every post carries a UTC+7 offset—the time zone for Bangkok, as well as Hanoi, Jakarta, and Phnom Penh.

In a recent development, every edit also carries a second fingerprint: The computer saving the changes has an internal clock that runs a few seconds fast. That consistent drift highlights that the same machine has been used for every post, which suggests that a single person could be updating the site.

Industry observers note that though IILA states on its website that it is a 501(c)(3), the IRS has no record of it, and it has no California registration. Instead, Colorado records list an “International Institute of Literature and Arts” as a nonprofit corporation registered in August 2025 at the address of a virtual mailbox service in Denver. It’s had a “delinquent” status since late August. (A local Denver newspaper ran a story in May asking why “over 12,000 different businesses all use” this same address.).

Sources indicate that several of the other organizations that use that same Colorado address, including the National Academy of Artificial Intelligence, the International Institute of Film Science & Arts, and the International Institute of Engineering Psychology (IIEP), were the subject of a Nature investigation in September. Nature’s reporting found that these organizations boasted high-ranking academics as their members, oftentimes without their knowledge or consent. According to Nature, the name most frequently associated with these organizations was Michael Chu, whose Chinese name, Chaoyang Zhu, is also listed as the incorporator of IILA in public records.

Yale University boasts one of the top ranked English departments in the world.

Chu’s name was previously listed on IILA’s website where Julian Lee’s name now appears, and his biography, according to another now deleted webpage, recovered through the Wayback Machine, includes a stint at another fake university that appears to belong to the same network, the City University of Colorado.

In response to a request for comment, IILA’s secretariat sent VF a series of unsigned emails, the first of which said the organization’s Colorado address was just an “early transitional filing point” and that a move to a “latest regional and national headquarters is right now underway.” The “delinquent” status, they wrote, merely “reflects an administrative transition delay between entities.”.

Another email stated that “we don’t know” about the other Chu-linked organizations mentioned in Nature’s report or why they all shared the same address.

According to recent reports, “What’s the matter with Michael Chu? He is not working here at present. I can’t contact him at present,” the secretariat wrote, before passing along Chu’s email.

Industry observers note that chu swiftly responded to Vanity Fair in both Chinese and English to “prevent misunderstandings.” “I have no contact with the Chinese government at present” and “I am not related to IILA at present, and I am not responsible for any work of IILA,” Chu wrote. He then went on to speculate about the questions regarding IILA’s legitimacy: “IILA is an organization registered according to law, but because the previous registered agency company remarked that there was a problem with the agency address, it needs to be re-registered. This may be the reason why some people think IILA is illegal.”.

“I think the supervision of the media is good and necessary, but we can’t use the power of the media to deliberately hinder normal academic exchanges,” posited Chu regarding the Nature article, which he says “many professors” he works with called “inexplicable and absurd.".

Nature did not respond to a request for comment in time for publication.

Asked to comment on IILA's connection with China, a Chinese embassy spokesperson said, “I am not familiar with the specific situation you mentioned.".

Last month, César Pablo Domínguez Prieto, a professor of comparative literature at the University of Santiago de Compostela in Spain, found himself going down a similar rabbit hole after he was invited by IILA to give a talk for an online seminar series titled “Newly introduced Directions in World and Comparative Literature” and promised an “Outstanding Speaker Award.”.

According to recent reports, “This solicitation prompted me to review their platform, where I discovered that the names and academic credentials of several of you are at the moment listed on their website,” Prieto wrote in an email to a group of his peers, which included Cornell’s Jonathan Dwight Culler, Harvard’s David Damrosch, and Shanghai Jiao Tong University’s Wang Ning. “The list includes other colleagues with whom I’m not acquainted.”.

Suspicious of the site and the invitation, Prieto dug further, finding those same public records that revealed Zhu’s name and the Colorado delinquent status.

Damrosch, a professor of world and comparative literature, was horrified to learn that his name was still being used by IILA without his “knowledge or permission.” He says he had written to them weeks ago asking for his name to be removed, with no result. (It has since been removed.).

“I suspect it is organized by the Chinese to place Chinese scholars in the organization of distinguished Western scholars, but it is all a bit of a mystery,” Culler, a professor of English and comparative literature, tells me.

“I checked, and you’re right! I am a fellow there,” Moretti, a literary scholar, responded when I asked if he knowingly accepted the fellowship from IILA.

Founded in 1896, Shanghai Jiao Tong University is one of China's top public universities.

Yale has since deleted its announcement of Newell’s honorary IILA fellowship amid her concerns about the academy’s legitimacy. Shanghai Jiao Tong University, however, proudly displays comparative literature professor Wang Ning’s honor on its website, congratulating him on his fellowship and on receiving “the Global Laureate Award in Literature and Cultural Theory.” A magazine sponsored and supervised by the Chinese National Academy of Arts under the Ministry of Culture and Tourism similarly applauded Wang’s IILA award in October.

In a recent development, “This organization’s business model relies on unilaterally placing the names of highly respected scholars—such as yourselves—on their website without informed or explicit consent, while using targeted invitations for seminar series like the one I received as a fishing hook,” Prieto alleged in the email to his colleagues. “They use your collective prestige to look legitimate, allowing them to target early-career researchers and charge them annual membership fees ranging from $95 to $175 USD for worthless certificates.” (The membership pricing that previously appeared on IILA’s website has apparently been removed.).

Prieto’s assessment of what might be driving this scam was in line with Nature’s reporting: While the journal remarked it “has not identified anyone who has admitted paying for” any awards or titles from the academic societies, sources interviewed for that article theorized that they are designed to attract younger professors in China who might be willing to pay to be in the company of more highly esteemed academics.

But experts who spoke to Vanity Fair suggested there might be something else more nefarious at play.

Jeff Fields, a fellow at the UC Berkeley Institute for Security and Governance who spent more than 20 years with the FBI, most recently as the assistant special agent in charge of counterintelligence at the FBI’s San Francisco field office, says he’s familiar with this type of scheme.

“One of the things they like to do,” Fields says of the Chinese government, “is to fabricate these associations that they then use to leverage for more sophisticated operations.”.

He has seen Chinese intelligence play such a long game, that it will spend years exaggerating or inventing affiliations in case it ever needs them, whether to lend someone credibility or to reach a particular target. If an agent later wants to get close to a professor who is friends with a certain researcher, for instance, the initial connections are already in place.

Jake Braun, who served as the White House’s acting principal deputy national cyber director under Joe Biden, agrees with Fields’s analysis, citing what’s known as the “thousand grains of sand” theory of Chinese intelligence. Because of its massive population, China has the ability to deploy an extraordinary number of people in its information-gathering techniques. Some might not necessarily be intelligence officers, he indicates, but each one can collect a single “grain of sand” of intelligence, which, when put together, works as an extremely powerful and effective intelligence apparatus.

Newell says that she was prompted on IILA’s website to create an account using her email address and a password, though once she was logged in, the website appeared entirely the same. Neither Fields nor Braun seemed terribly concerned about the possibility that those passwords could be used by whoever was behind the website to try to hack into the professors’ university accounts or emails.

What’s more likely, states Braun, is that in addition to the long game of network-building for future intelligence operations, IILA may also double as a platform to lend credibility to misinformation and disinformation campaigns by associating them with reputable scholars—another tactic he’s seen used before to influence narratives about China at the West’s foremost universities.

In a recent development, the Chinese professors listed as IILA fellows primarily come from three public, and therefore government-funded, universities, all in Shanghai: Fudan University, Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU), and Shanghai University. In July 2026, the US Department of Defense added Fudan University and SJTU to a list of academic and research institutions deemed “a concern to national security.”.

Recent findings suggest that SJTU had already come under scrutiny following a 2023 incident in which five Chinese students enrolled in its joint program with the University of Michigan allegedly photographed military exercises at a National Guard training facility in the state. The students were charged in October 2024 with making false statements and related offenses, months after they left the country following graduation, according to the federal complaint. Three months later, the university announced the termination of its two-decade partnership with SJTU, citing national security concerns. (The partnership is still featured on SJTU’s website, however.).

Sources indicate that fudan University, meanwhile, was involved in the recent high-profile spying case of former Federal Reserve employee John Rodgers, who allegedly funneled classified government information to a spy he met at a conference in China. Rodgers would later send sensitive information to a Fudan professor and become a teacher there himself after leaving the Fed. (In July, he was sentenced to 38 months in federal prison for making false statements to federal investigators about sharing restricted Federal Reserve information with Chinese intelligence operatives.).

Wang Ning of Shanghai Jiao Tong University feels certain that IILA is legitimate.

Still, Damrosch notes that those schools are also home to the leading literature programs in China, so their inclusion on the list does make sense from an academic perspective.

Because of their positions at public universities in China, some of the professors listed alongside Newell and her colleagues on IILA’s list of fellows also have ties to the Chinese Communist Party. Wang, for example, is the dean of SJTU’s Institute of Arts and Humanities, which houses a research hub, jointly established by Shanghai’s municipal CCP publicity department, focused on China’s international image. And, in 2023, he spearheaded the launch of a upcoming cultural research center at SJTU dedicated to China’s “united front” work, which the US-China Economic and Security Review Commission has described as being used “to co-opt and neutralize sources of potential opposition to the policies and authority of its ruling Chinese Communist Party.”.

When I reach out to Wang, he is eager to talk, noting that he knows “Vanity Fair is a prestigious popular journal in the United States.” We meet over Zoom, which he joins from an empty room in Beijing with one overhead light.

He tells me he received Prieto’s email, but he believes his colleague is mistaken and feels certain that IILA is legitimate. Wang insists that the members he has nominated from his own university were not asked to pay any fee. He indicates he’s communicated with both Michael Chu and Julian Lee, and that he doesn’t actually think it matters that he’s never met them. What affords the academy authenticity, says Wang, is its members and their own accomplishments, which are real and impressive—on that part, at least, everyone is in agreement.

“Oh, please let them be Chinese spies, please,” Newell says of IILA’s leadership. “That would be one of the best things ever in my whole life.” She finds the whole thing very amusing, needing to pause in the middle of our interview for a laugh break.

“I love the idea of fooling top academics,” indicates Newell. “I think it’s hilarious that we’re so famous, that our egos…the fact that none of us questioned getting awards and fellowships and we’re all so eagerly accepting them and letting our universities know how clever we are…I mean, it’s hilarious, and pathetic, and it says so much about the profession.”.

It was looking like there really wouldn't be any way out of the danger Irwin (Miles Teller), his brother Gary (Adam Driver) and his family were in. Gary, as it turned out, wasn't the kind of cop who would cross major ethical lines by working with the Russian mob - at least not for any kind of job that isn't above board. When money wasn't going to be enough to satisfy Simeon Bogoyavich (Victor Ptak), and Gary wasn't willing to work with him, the only way to make things right was for Gary to accept the terms of Simeon's deal: his life in exchange for his brother's (and his family's) safety. That was Simeon's price, and Gary agreed to pay it.

After seeing his brother one last time at Scott's birthday party, Gary lies and says he's leaving the country, assuring Irwin things are going to be ok and gifting him his car. We see him get emotional when he's by himself in his rental car, which I interpret as him accepting his fate, as terrible as it is.

Later, he drives toward the airport and waits until he sees the Russian guys tailing him. He mutters something about wanting to take them out with him, and then pulls off to the side of the road, where he hides in a nearby field. The guys creep around among the stalks and Gary shoots a couple of them, the gunshot sounds muffled by the planes overhead. He's inevitably shot by one of them and dies.

Sources indicate that at Irwin's house, his wife Hester (Scarlett Johansson) has snuck off to have surgery on her brain tumor. She's last seen blowing a kiss to her husband and kids, who are still asleep. Later that morning, Scott is helping Ben study, and Irwin listens to a message about job opportunities now that his and his brother's consulting business is registered. The tone is uplifting in the Pearl house, despite what we know. Does this mean that everything is going to be ok, and the Russian mob boss will keep his end of the deal now that Gary is dead?

As writer/director James Gray told us, he has hope that things will be ok for the family.

Recent findings suggest that I think they're going to be all right. Somehow I have hope. You get he gets a message that this the better business or the business bureau or whatever it is, is going to has all this great jobs lined up for him and his children are studying for school very dutifully.

Industry observers note that in the final scene within the Pearl house, they don't yet know about Hester's situation, though it seems unlikely that she'll keep that a secret for long. This family may be out of the woods with this Russian mob situation, but that doesn't mean everything will be perfect in the coming weeks and months. As Gray put it:.

Your Daily Blend of Entertainment News.

It has been revealed that I mean, he's got something terrible coming with his wife that he doesn't know about, right? But that's life. You know, bad things and good things happen in equal measure. We almost have to kind of accept that that's what our fates are as human beings. But I think he'll be all right.

The more I think about Paper Tiger's ending, the more this makes sense to me and adds to my overall satisfaction to this suspenseful and emotional film. Hester's tumor is nobody's doing, just the tragic nature of life, unfair though it may be. So much of what transpired in the film had to do with choices and actions, but in the case of Hester, it's just the cards she was dealt, and she and her family will have to face that.

I did personally feel a note of hope in that final scene. Because Irwin and his sons weren't aware of what happened to Gary, or what was going in with Hester, they were just going about their morning routines. It felt like we were seeing a glimpse of what everyday life would look like for these three Pearl men, and it was simple and safe. It's the calm before another storm, but there's a note of optimism that they'll get through it and have each other for support.

At present, she’s an Assistant Managing Editor who spends much of her time brainstorming and editing features, analyzing site data, working with writers and editors on content planning and the workflow, and obsessing over the best movies and TV highlights. She graduated from SUNY Cortland with BA in Communication Studies and a minor in Cinema Studies. When she isn't working, she's probably thinking about work, or reading (or listening to a book), and making sure her cats are living their absolute best feline lives.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

David Fincher, the director of "Seven," "Fight Club," and many other classic films, very nearly had a major influence on "Star Wars" before Disney took control of the franchise. So, what would he have done with one of the most popular sci-fi properties on the planet? He would have focused on a pair of beloved characters, specifically the best droids in the "Star Wars" property.

Recent findings suggest that on a recent episode of the "Happy Sad Confused" podcast, Fincher revealed that he had a conversation with former Lucasfilm President Kathleen Kennedy about taking th studio public before Disney bought Lucasfilm in 2012. But what would Fincher have done with "Star Wars" had that panned out? Perhaps not what you'd expect.

His interest lay with C-3PO and R2-D2, primarily. Not Luke Skywalker. Not Princess Leia. A protocol droid and his astromech companion. And while Fincher admitted he didn't have a full pitch, he did have a rough idea. Here's what he had to say:.

"I stated, 'The thing that has always interested me about — certainly from the first movie — was the relationship between [C-]3PO and R2[-D2]. That they were essentially slaves who would bear witness to the folly of man. I always thought that, them being captured by Jawas, and then sold off and being on the periphery and witnessing the Skywalker Saga, was such a crucial element to it. [...] There was a kind of moral judgment. It was fairly obvious even from 3PO [...] he had a kind of understanding as to what the Empire meant, how evil they were.".

"He was kind of trying to decide whether or not he wanted to invest in having a relationship with Luke Skywalker when he's getting his oil bath [in 'A New Hope'], and they're talking," Fincher added.

Industry observers note that "Even from ['The Empire Strikes Back'], when 3PO is turned back on, and he recounts for you what he sees with the stormtroopers already being in [...] Bespin," David FIncher continued. "Whenever they used the robots for that, I was always really excited. I always thought that was kind of interesting, that you have to go through the recorder, like the court reporter, to find out what it is that happened.".

In a recent development, notably, C-3PO actor Anthony Daniels is the only actor to appear in all nine main "Star Wars" movies, while Kenny Baker portrayed R2-D2 in the original trilogy. These are characters who certainly have earned time in the spotlight, but using them as the crux of a latest era for the franchise? That's a strange idea.

Sources indicate that be that as it may, Fincher and Kathleen Kennedy were interested in seeing if they could make something happen. Fincher, however, revealed that Disney's purchase of Lucasfilm (a deal that encompassed $4 billion in cash and stocks) nixed those plans. As the filmmaker recalled:.

"I noted to [Kennedy], I kind of pitched her this idea, I said, 'Let's take this thing to Wall Street and let the market decide.' And I think it was a month later or something, she said, 'Bad news. Apparently there's a $7 billion offer on the table,' and I said, 'We're not going to beat that.'".

George Lucas later opened up about selling Lucafilm to Disney, describing it as "very, very painful." Of course, it proved to be enormously beneficial for Disney, financially speaking. Fincher, meanwhile, has gone on to continue enjoying a very fruitful career outside the confines of a galaxy far, far away.
