📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some people collect works of art; others collect clothes. When I heard about a Parisian who had amassed thousands of Ralph Lauren pieces, my curiosity got the better of me and I wanted to learn more. Séverin Naudet, a former digital adviser to François Fillon when he was France’s prime minister, lives on the fifth floor of a beautiful Haussmann-style building. The tall, dark-haired 50-year-old appears not to age. Since leaving his role with the government in 2012, he has started a digital marketing firm and is now also exploring opportunities in luxury and wellness.

At his home, he displays part of his wardrobe, and I realize that the rumors about Naudet are true. He shows me dozens of pairs of sneakers, tuxedo jackets and velvet shoes, pants and shirts, more jackets, and then there are also mugs, books, and pillows. In the bedroom, the linens bear the American designer’s label, while tableware from Ralph Lauren’s Burleigh Collection, carefully wrapped up and placed in a Carrefour bag, is ready to be taken to his house in Brittany, where “more sailboat-inspired” pieces are stored. There are also sorbet-colored swimsuits piled on the plump armrests of a club chair. “About 20 years ago I donated all my other clothes to a charity. Since then, I’ve worn nothing but Ralph Lauren,” he explains, barefoot and dressed in jeans and a Polo shirt, next to a jacket from Denim & Supply, a Ralph Lauren brand that existed from 2011 to 2016 and is now coveted by collectors. Naudet’s Ralph Lauren pieces represent more than just a wardrobe; they embody a way of life that embraces every facet of the American brand founded in 1967—from preppy cool to sophisticated, Gatsby-style chic, and including many nautical pieces that connect to another of Naudet’s passions: sailing.

A selection from his collection of sneakers and dress shoes.

It has been revealed that but how does one fall in love with a brand to the point of making it part of every facet of their life? “As a teenager, I had body image challenges. I had bowlegs, and I didn’t feel comfortable in my own skin,” he explains. Walking into a Double RL store changed everything: “I tried on a pair of Low Straight jeans and it was magical—they were perfectly cut, elegant, and stylish. I almost felt sexy. I had straight legs and a nice butt,” he claims with a laugh.

Industry observers note that his connection to the American brand speaks volumes about that magic formula that is the goal of retailers around the world: combining storytelling with emotional attachment. “Polo was the cure for a certain melancholy that was the result of a gloomy childhood. Ralph Lauren instilled in me a spirit of joy, where yellows, pinks, and sky blues, stripes and madras fabrics, evoke summer, the sea, and sailing,” explains the man who has amassed several thousand Ralph Lauren items.

Industry observers note that as retail experiences increasingly take place online, there’s nothing Naudet loves more than going to a physical store. Walking into one is like stepping into “the family home I never had,” he explains. “A Ralph Lauren flagship store can feel like visiting a house in the Hamptons, a Parisian hotel for a perfect Christmas, or a Newly introduced York apartment with a view of Central Park.” Ralph Lauren locations are must-visits on the entrepreneur’s itineraries. In Manhattan, he always visits the West Broadway store. He knows, of course, the ones in London and Los Angeles, as well as Manda in Brussels, where he goes in search of vintage pieces. His favorite store, however, remains the one in the mansion on Boulevard Saint-Germain in Paris, where every year he celebrates Christmas at its Ralph’s restaurant.

According to recent reports, one might call him a “perfectionist,” but he prefers “meticulous.” He will go to lengths to repair clothes, even if it requires tracking down the original fabrics or finding an expert to repair braided leather straps. He’s also interested in the story behind the brand and how design choices and corporate strategies have made it what it is today. “Ralph Lauren is a marketing genius, and his advertising is never simply advertising. He works instead like a filmmaker; he tells a story. All you need is an image, even without a product. He created a family that we all dream of being a part of by, for example, choosing his wife, Ricky, as his muse. Their marriage has lasted 60 years!” the former adviser shares. And at a time when the world is wondering and worrying about the future, Ralph Lauren and his mythologies are calm and soothing: “In a daily life saturated with screens, images, and now artificial intelligence, Ralph Lauren continues to offer a world that is profoundly real, tactile, and inhabited.” The proof? In a fashion world sometimes tinged with gloom, Ralph Lauren posted a 15% increase in revenue for 2025, surpassing $8 billion for the first time. And in the first quarter of 2026, growth continued strong at 14%.

In a recent development, he quotes from memory Tocqueville’s description of Latest England in 1835 as “a region left to the dreams of the imagination, which one ought to abandon to the free trials of innovators.” Ralph Lauren is, for Naudet, the brand that stands above the fray, its founder a dreamer embodying “the finest qualities of the United States, from Tocqueville to the present day.” We ask if, as the ultimate embodiment of the American dream, Ralph Lauren, 86, would make a good president? Naudet, an expert on the inner workings of power, smiles: “He possesses at least three key qualities needed to be a good president: He understands the times, he has broad appeal, and he inspires people to dream. The rest is part of the mystery of democracy, and America is a great democracy.”.

It has been revealed that if the self-made New Yorker has ever wondered who his biggest fan in France is, Vanity Fair has found him. Before our conversation ends, Naudet tells me that recently, as he does every year around this time, he bought two pairs of Heritage Straight jeans, and also spotted a leather jacket lined with shearling that he wanted. It’s “admittedly a bit pricey,” but he’s certain it’ll be perfect once the temperatures drop.

Blade Runner 2099 Revives A Major Element From Philip K. Dick's Original Novel

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (883 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Slashfilm

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Any fan of "Blade Runner" knows that the source material for the film, Philip K.
  • To be fair, "Blade Runner" retains a surprising amount of Dick's novel, with whole swathes of dialogue making it all the way from the author's page to the screen.
  • According to recent reports, this idea didn't make it to "Blade Runner" in any shape or form, however it does appear (and largely intact, too) in this month's "Blade Runner 2099" sequel series.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Any fan of "Blade Runner" knows that the source material for the film, Philip K. Dick's novel "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?," didn't exactly make it to the significant screen fully intact. As influential and unique as it is, Dick's work proved too unwieldy for filmmakers to adapt wholesale. Instead, Hollywood took Dick's themes and concepts and heavily rewrote his stories for the screen. That trend began with "Blade Runner," as original screenwriter Hampton Fancher took the neo-noir concept from Dick's trippy, weird 1968 novel of a human hunting down illegal androids and pretty much discarded the rest. The relationship between "Androids" and "Blade Runner" can be succinctly summed up by the fact that Fancher and director Ridley Scott didn't use Dick's title for the film, eventually going so far as to borrow the title from a completely different novel by William S. Burroughs.

To be fair, "Blade Runner" retains a surprising amount of Dick's novel, with whole swathes of dialogue making it all the way from the author's page to the screen. Yet numerous other plot elements and characters were either altered or omitted altogether. One element in "Androids" which is very vital to Dick's worldbuilding is the concept of Mercerism, a religion in which devotees share a looping, pre-programmed experience via a virtual reality machine called an empathy box.

According to recent reports, this idea didn't make it to "Blade Runner" in any shape or form, however it does appear (and largely intact, too) in this month's "Blade Runner 2099" sequel series. The use of Mercerism in the Prime Video show is a great example of showrunner Silka Luisa and her writers knowing Dick and "Blade Runner" well. In fact, the inclusion of a missing element of Dick's novel in a "Blade Runner" sequel is a bit of a franchise tradition.

In "Blade Runner 2099," it initially seems that Silka Luisa and company have included Mercerism as a little Easter egg, as a couple of animated billboards in Los Angeles advertise it. Yet this isn't a winking reference to Philip K. Dick's novel, but is instead foreshadowing. In Episode 6, entitled "Kill the Killers," Cora (Hunter Schafer) and Olwen (Michelle Yeoh) travel to a hideaway where Cora and her brother grew up. It turns out this hideaway is a defunct Mercer Monastery, a place where those who worship the man could come to and use an empathy box or interact with automated priest-like programs (shades of George Lucas' "THX 1138" there).

Mercerism, as detailed in Dick's "Androids," is a religion based around the idea of increasing empathy, since the future of the novel has become so dystopian and isolating that people need to be reminded to have empathy for others (sound familiar?). This is done through the empathy box, which allows owners to experience a moment from the life of Wilbur Mercer, apparently some kind of martyr. In the box, Mercer endlessly climbs up a hill while being pelted with rocks, and the "empathy" the user experiences is holding onto sensors which deliver increasingly harsher shocks, sometimes resulting in death.

In a recent development, the idea was first introduced by Dick in a short story in 1964 entitled "The Little Black Box," and then re-used in "Androids." The ironic twist in "Androids" is that Mercerism is revealed to be a total sham, with the video loop having been shot on a soundstage with an actor. Though this isn't addressed in "2099," the obvious decline in Mercerites and decay of the monastery implies that the religion isn't as popular as it once was.

Even though Mercerism didn't make it into a previous iteration of "Blade Runner," the themes behind it are so integral to the story of "Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep?" and its world that its inclusion feels natural. "Blade Runner 2099" smoothly weaves it into its storyline, using it as an allegory for its doomed principal characters as well as its apocalyptic vision of Earth in general. It's used in the show in much the same way Dick uses it in "Androids," as a satiric commentary on how what was initially intended as an aspirational endeavor has devolved into something more pathetic than never believing in it in the first place.

Ironically, Mercerism is not the first element in "Androids" that was left out of "Blade Runner" but made a return appearance in a sequel story to Ridley Scott's film. In "Androids," the character of John R. Isidore (or J.R. Isidore) was reconceived and rewritten as J.F. Sebastian for "Blade Runner," and he was killed during the events of the film. However, when Dick's friend K.W. Jeter wrote the 1995 novel "Blade Runner 2: The Edge of Human," Jeter brought J.R. Isidore back into the story. It's not entirely clear if Jeter intends his Isidore to be the literal same character, or if he's "borrowing" the character in the same manner as Dick borrowed Mercerism from his short story for "Androids." Either way, it established a neat little tradition for the franchise, in which anything or anyone could come back, and perhaps come back different. For a series infamous for characters not ever fully knowing their true identity and heritage, the tradition feels rather poignant.

"Blade Runner 2099" is now streaming on Prime Video.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With just over a week before Fortnite Treasure Hunters comes to an end, desperation has set in, as players begin to lose hope of finding the Pirate Shop Access token. This is the most coveted item in Fortnite history because it grants up to 28 days of free Item Shop cosmetics.

The long search for the token has driven players to cheat. Epic Games has managed to catch these cheaters red-handed and has publicly unveiled that it will be banning them from Fortnite.

The consequences aren't limited to the players who resorted to cheating software. Players who win the token by teaming up with a cheater will not be banned, but they will be stripped of the token as well as any Item Shop goodies they claimed while it was active — even if they were unaware that a person in their party cheated. Players who teamed up with the cheater via Squad Fills are the only exception. This measure aims to prevent players from creating a smurf account exclusively for cheating.

Industry observers note that the Pirate Shop Access token may be a reward that's almost too good to be true, but it's also extremely rare. The odds of finding the token are low (0.000007273%). Some players have opened over 150,000 chests with no luck, so it can definitely be frustrating to continue on. Players' best bet is to keep searching and collect other treasure from chests along the way.

In a recent development, with Golden Week coming up on Nov. 28, players will at least have increased chances of finding the rare gilded skins. Additionally, the week-long event begins on Saturday, when the final Treasure Hours of the season will be active, cranking up token odds by 1.5x. Fortnite Treasure Hunters ends on Dec. 5, so players still have some time to open chests and get the token before it's vaulted for good.

#120130. What’s Real and What’s Not in Netflix’s ‘The Altruists’

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1155 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Vanityfair ↗ Open Full Page

What’s Real and What’s Not in Netflix’s ‘The Altruists’

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1155 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vanityfair

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Even if you followed the news closely in the early 2020s, the sheer audacity of the fraud committed by Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison—as dramatized in Netflix’s latest limited series The Altruists, starring Anthony Boyle and Julia Garner—will shock you anew.
  • Recent findings suggest that I found the series to be especially striking in the context of last week’s historic Anthropic IPO, which ironically fell on the same day as the premiere.
  • The Altruists also depicts a surprisingly tender romance between two socially inept, possibly sociopathic adrenaline junkies.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Even if you followed the news closely in the early 2020s, the sheer audacity of the fraud committed by Sam Bankman-Fried and Caroline Ellison—as dramatized in Netflix’s latest limited series The Altruists, starring Anthony Boyle and Julia Garner—will shock you anew. The show, which follows the stunning multibillion-dollar collapse of the crypto exchange FTX, starts off a bit slow, but accelerates episode by episode until its high-octane finale.

Recent findings suggest that I found the series to be especially striking in the context of last week’s historic Anthropic IPO, which ironically fell on the same day as the premiere. Some of that organization’s founders and employees share similar intellectual roots to The Altruist’s protagonists; watching its fictionalized Caroline Ellison, in particular, justify astoundingly reckless behavior with her system of mathematical-optimization-of-everything felt uncannily like watching frontier labs proceed with a seemingly inexplicable appetite for risk.

The Altruists also depicts a surprisingly tender romance between two socially inept, possibly sociopathic adrenaline junkies. (According to people involved with the project, the working title for the project was Untitled Love Story.) But as with any fictionalized account, the series takes some liberties with the characters and plot. If you’re anything like me, you want to know what exactly is fact, and what is fiction.

I spoke with Kevin T. Dugan and Jen Wieczner, two of the reporters who exposed the FTX fiasco in real time, and who consulted on the series. “When Jen and I started working with Graham Moore, the showrunner, he made it really clear that he wanted this to be very character driven. Nobody wants an eight-hour lecture on how the blockchain works,” Dugan tells me.

Sources indicate that “The bones of the show are rooted in reality,” states Wieczner. Understanding these flawed and complicated characters helps explain “how one decision leads to another decision and a small oopsies turns into a multibillion-dollar fraud and this huge criminal conspiracy.”.

Even if there’s a little fiction in the nitty-gritty, Dugan says that there is one overarching truth he hopes the series will reveal: “That even the prettiest ideas still have to turn into reality through imperfect people, and those imperfect people will end up making mistakes that they cannot foresee.” Here’s what the show ripped from real life—and where it took some creative license.

CAROLINE ELLISON WROTE SEXY HARRY POTTER FAN FICTION.

Not quite. In the first episode, Caroline is humiliated when her raunchy writing titled “A Ride on Draco’s Nimbus” surfaces online. And while it’s true that Ellison was a huge Harry Potter fan, there is no evidence she wrote erotic fan fiction herself. Instead, this plot point is likely gesturing toward Ellison’s 2010s-era Tumblr, which was called WorldOptimisation—a reference to a 660,000-word-long work of Harry Potter fan fiction by Silicon Valley philosopher Eliezer Yudkowsky. Yudkowsky’s work popularized the kind of mathematically strategic thinking Ellison applies to love and business alike.

SAM TRABUCCO’S “INFINITE MONEY HACK”.

It has been revealed that in episode six, Sam Trabucco (played by Alex Lawther) makes the mistake of introducing Sam and Caroline to a hack that proves irresistible: FTX can mint its own coin, FTT, and then allow its crypto trading firm, Alameda, to take out large loans using off-market FTT as collateral. Alameda can then use those loans to place highly leveraged, incredibly risky bets on FTX—which in turn increases the value of FTT. (TL;DR: it’s a perfect loop.) Appalling as it sounds, in real life, this practice is more or less exactly what brought SBF’s empire tumbling down.

“One of the things that led to the FTX bank run,” explains Wieczner, “was the leaked balance sheet that demonstrated that much of FTX and Alameda’s holdings were in FTT, which was FTX’s own coin. So that if that went to zero, it was like a house of cards and things just would’ve fallen apart. And that’s why you see at the end why is everything is falling…you have that kind of death spiral effect.”.

Industry observers note that as for Trabucco, he and his yacht (yes, it was really named Soak My Deck) didn’t get off unscathed. Trabucco didn’t face criminal charges, but was forced to liquidate many of his assets in order to help return about $80 million to defrauded investors.

CAROLINE ELLISON WAS INTO POLYAMORY.

True. Caroline chronicled some of her adventures in nonmonogamy on her since-deleted Tumblr. She once wrote, “The only acceptable style of poly is best characterized as something like ‘imperial Chinese harem.’”.

Real! In the final episode of the series, SBF presents a last-ditch initiative: He wants to repurpose his early stake in Anthropic to cover the losses of billions of dollars in customer funds. Indeed, FTX did use $500 million in customer funds to purchase a 13.5% stake in Anthropic’s Series B in late 2021. Of course, Sam’s plan did not pass muster. Yet if it had, he’d have been in the clear. After the tech giant’s IPO last week, Alameda’s stake would be worth about $35 billion, according to The New York Times—enough to solve the disgraced firm’s liquidity issues several times over. Oh well.

CAROLINE ELLISON CONFESSED IN FRONT OF HER STAFF.

It has been revealed that true. In the penultimate episode, a visibly cracking Caroline delivers a halting confession amidst fits of nervous giggles to a shocked staff, telling them that she knew about FTX’s shortfall of user funds that would add up to more than $8 billion. I was sure this scene had been invented, but lo and behold: Ellison did admit that she had been aware of the inappropriate transfers between the two firms at a December 2022 all-staff meeting. You can even listen to the leaked recording online.

CAROLINE ELLISON BEARS MORE RESPONSIBILITY THAN SBF.

I felt the show tilted towards placing the blame on Ellison, who is portrayed as incorrigibly risk-addicted and the muse behind SBF’s worst decisions. Constance Wang, who is played in the series by Madison Hu, is just one of the former FTX employees who found the show misrepresentative. In a lengthy X post, she rebutted its narrative: Ellison, said Hu, “wasn’t nearly that reckless, and she was never the one pushing to go all in. The idea that she was the mastermind behind everything made us laugh.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, "Avatar" fans can thank Eywa, because more sequels are indeed coming. As reported by Collider, Disney's upcoming film release slate includes "Avatar 4" (dated for December 21, 2029) and "Avatar 5" (dated for December 19, 2031). These dates aren't necessarily etched in stone; during the 2010s, the release date for "Avatar: The Way of Water" got pushed back so much that many convinced themselves the movie was never coming out. You simply can't rush the quality that director James Cameron demands of the "Avatar" films. But it's a sign Disney wants the movies out sooner than later.

Was the future of a billion dollar franchise like "Avatar" ever in doubt? Keep in mind, the third movie, 2025's "Avatar: Fire and Ash," was the lowest grossing movie in the series. It still grossed just under $1.5 billion, but that's a notably diminished return next to "The Way of Water," which pulled $2.3 billion internationally. "Fire and Ash" was also, like its predecessors, one of the most expensive movies ever made.

It has been revealed that there's also the fact that director James Cameron, who has spent decades immersed in the world of Pandora, wants to direct other projects. Cameron is right now working on "Ghosts of Hiroshima," based on the non-fiction book by author Charles Pellegrino, and he's likewise attached to an adaptation of Joe Abercrombie's dark fantasy book "The Devils.".

Industry observers note that cameron, who is 72 years old, is in the stage of his life where he has to balance the films he wants to make against the time he has left, and he knows it. As he told the Empire Film podcast back in May 2026, he wants to make the fourth and fifth "Avatar" films in less time, and for less money, than it took to make "The Way of Water" and "Fire and Ash.".

James Cameron told People in 2023 that "Avatar 4" will feature a six-year time jump. Parts of the film were even shot concurrently with "Fire and Ash" to capture the series' younger actors, like Jack Champion (Spider) and Trinity Bliss (Tuktirey), while they still pass as kids.

Sources indicate that the "Avatar" films have strong environmentalist themes; humanity wants to colonize Pandora because, by the 22nd century, Earth is polluted, overpopulated, and seemingly dying. We've only seen small glimpses of that in the previous films. Producer Jon Landau told Syfy back in 2023 that "Avatar 4" will change that:.

"There's over-population and a depletion of our natural resources that make life harder. But we don't want to paint a bleak picture for where our world is going. The films are also about the idea of that we can change course.".

It has been revealed that what about lingering threads on Pandora? "Fire and Ash" ended with the recombinant Colonel Miles Quaritch (Stephen Lang) seemingly plummeting to his death. But one of the most essential rules of fiction is if you don't see a dead body, and sometimes even if you do, don't treat mortal peril as confirmed death.

Quaritch already beat death once, and it feels like he still hasn't quite completed his story yet. Even if Lang/Quaritch does sit "Avatar 4" out, "Fire and Ash" ended with his accomplice Varang (Oona Chaplin) still at large. Varang was easily the breakout character of "Fire and Ash," and I'd be shocked if we don't see her return to attack the Sully family again in movie number four.

"Avatar 4" is right now scheduled for theatrical release on December 21, 2029.

Duran Duran has confirmed the death of its iconic guitarist Andy Taylor “following a long and courageous battle with prostate cancer.” He was 65.

“Andy passed away peacefully at home, surrounded by family, on Monday 23rd November,” the “Hungry Like the Wolf” band declared in a Wednesday, November 25, statement.

Sources indicate that andy became one of the classic “Fab Five” members of Duran Duran when he joined the New Wave band in 1980, along with singer Simon Le Bon, keyboardist Nick Rhodes, drummer Roger Taylor and bassist John Taylor. (Andy, Roger, 66, and John, 66, were not related.).

Sources indicate that the group went on to sell more than 100 million records worldwide and received a coveted star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame in 1993. They were inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2022. (Andy left Duran Duran originally in 1986 but later returned for a five-year reunion stint between 2001 to 2006.).

Andy was also part of the 1980s supergroup the Power Station, along with Duran Duran bandmate John, Chic drummer Tony Thompson and frontman Robert Palmer. Formed in 1984, the Power Station scored U.S. Top 10 hits with “Some Like It Hot” and a cover for T. Rex’s “Get It On.”.

Le Bon, 68, confirmed during Duran Duran’s Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction ceremony in 2022 that Andy was unable to attend after being diagnosed with stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer.

“Andy was there at the very beginning of our story,” Duran Duran mentioned on Wednesday. “From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music. His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed.”.

The guitarist tied the knot with wife Tracey Wilson on the Sunset Strip in 1982 and they remained married until his death. They welcomed four children: Georgina, Isabella, Bethany, and Andrew.

“To the world, Andy was a brilliant guitarist, but to us, he was the most wonderful husband, a loving dad and the proudest grandfather. He was the rock of our family,” Tracey said in a Monday statement. “For all the incredible experiences music brought him, family always came first. Nothing made him happier than having us all together, and no matter how far music took him, his heart was always at home.”.

Recent findings suggest that she continued, “Andy faced the last few years with so much courage and determination. He never gave up, fighting until the very end, never losing his love of life. The kindness and support shown to him by fans from all over the world throughout his illness brought him immense comfort and strength, and for that we will always be grateful. Andy knew just how deeply he was loved, and we take great comfort in that. We will miss him every single day.”.

Andy’s Duran Duran bandmates each paid tribute to the late musician with individual and heartfelt statements, with Le Bon fondly highlighting the “blond bombshell, firebrand teenager” he met in 1980.

Recent findings suggest that “There’s a massive Andy Taylor shaped hole in my heart,” he wrote. “It’ll never close up; I won’t let it. I will miss him & love him for all my days.”.

John focused on Andy’s musicianship, describing him as a “demon” and a “killer riff-merchant, melodist, six string textualist.”.

  • In a recent development, after working at Politico, HuffPost, and The Intercept, Grim, 48, cofounded Drop Site News, an independent nonprofit news organization, in 2024, and he’s also a cohost on the antiestablishment political podcast Breaking Points.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anyone still struggling to understand how Bernie Bros and MAGA voters overlap on the political Venn diagram might find answers in Ryan Grim’s audience.

Grim, a veteran journalist and self-described “leftist,” has cultivated a rather politically diverse and incongruous fan base over his two decades in journalism. On election night in Los Angeles earlier this month, a room full of socialists erupted in cheers when Grim appeared on the big screen at the Democratic Socialists of America’s watch party (Grim was a guest that night on Hasan Piker’s livestream). The next day, a friend who religiously listens to Tim Dillon, a podcaster credited with helping Trump win reelection in 2024, and Tony Hinchcliffe, a comedian who performed at a Trump rally that same year, told me that he was also a huge fan of Grim’s.

In a recent development, after working at Politico, HuffPost, and The Intercept, Grim, 48, cofounded Drop Site News, an independent nonprofit news organization, in 2024, and he’s also a cohost on the antiestablishment political podcast Breaking Points. He’s developed a reputation for being an equal opportunity critic of both parties, which Grim claims helps explain why people all along the spectrum are attracted to his work. Even Steve Bannon (who called Grim an “intrepid reporter”) and former Republican congressman Matt Gaetz have occasionally thrown compliments his way.

“I think there’s a huge overlap with Breaking Points, Drop Site, and the whole podcast-bro world,” Grim tells Vanity Fair. “It does feel like we’ve basically become the primary news source for the podcast bros, which is not how you would have necessarily understood the world several years ago.”.

But lest anyone think that Grim has changed his views to accommodate newly introduced fans, his frequent criticism of Israel’s war in Gaza has helped make him a target of Fox News host Mark Levin, who has called into question Drop Site’s nonprofit status.

In a wide-ranging conversation, Grim discusses his unlikely popularity among the podcast bros, why he thinks the Epstein files helped propel Democrats in 2026, why he doesn’t understand the protests against Jerry Seinfeld, and what his favorite jam band, Phish, taught him about tolerance.

This conversation has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Industry observers note that vanity Fair: You’ve talked about how being a leftist rather than a Democratic partisan has helped you build credibility with conservatives. Why is that distinction vital?

Recent findings suggest that ryan Grim: [The conservatives] never thought I was a Democratic partisan, because I wasn’t. I think if you have a view of the world, people are willing to say, Okay, that’s his view of the world, and I’m going to metabolize what he’s reporting while taking into account that he has a particular view of the world.

But if you’re a partisan for Democrats or Republicans, that’s different because then you’re playing, like, strategic games with your information, and your view of whether or not something is good or bad changes with whether or not it’s good or bad for Democrats or good or bad for Republicans, rather than being grounded in some type of idea about the world.

And you’ve been criticizing Democrats for decades.

Yeah, I think what frustrates our critics is that they can’t be like, “Oh yeah, well, you didn’t say that when Biden was president or when Obama was president,” and it’s like, “Oh no, in fact, we remarked this and worse,” because it didn’t matter the color of the jersey. We believed that drone strikes were wrong, or shutting down ACORN is bad, and we’re going to say it no matter who’s in office.

According to recent reports, jeremy [Scahill] and I have been doing this for so long that we have that track record, so I think that has really helped us build that audience across the spectrum. It’s been pretty gratifying to develop that conservative audience. It’s weird sometimes to hear a Steve Bannon or a Matt Gaetz applauding your journalism. But it’s like, hey, that doesn't necessarily mean they agree with us about our conclusions. That’s not what we’re here for. We’re here to do the reporting.

You grew up around a lot of Moral Majority conservatives in rural Maryland, and you’ve said that even though you disagreed with their politics, you didn’t necessarily think they were bad people. Is that something the left has lost sight of?

They were almost universally pretty good people whose views I didn’t share as a young person and don’t now. But that’s just who they are.

I’ve talked to other people who still live in these rural areas, and they’re like, “How do I deal with these people who have these wretched beliefs?” I say, “Just deal with them as people.” They were kind of born believing that, and a lot of them are rethinking things all the time.

In a recent development, you seem to have a lot more patience for people you disagree with than some of your fellow leftists. How do you reconcile that with your own pretty uncompromising politics?

I try to live by the creed of [left-wing political commentator] Michael Brooks. He used to say, “Be ruthless to systems, be kind to people,” and that can be very hard. But to me the most important thing to do is try to understand that people operate within systems, and it is the system that you’re against, not the people.

I think you’re more likely to win converts by understanding what their role is in the system and keeping your criticisms at that systemic level.

Sources indicate that I think sometimes people go a little bit crazy. I don’t agree with Jerry Seinfeld’s politics when it comes to Israel, but I don’t understand the value of protesting Jerry Seinfeld. Maybe he’s given some money or something, but like, in general, he’s not a decision-maker. What is the upside in making him a target of protest? That part I don’t understand.

Speaking of people who disagree with you, Mark Levin has been going after Drop Site News’s nonprofit status. How seriously are you taking his efforts?

So if tomorrow Levin succeeded, and we were no longer a nonprofit, we would then carry on as a for-profit supported by our readers.

It has been revealed that I know the underlying hostility is he doesn’t like our reporting—he doesn’t want it to exist. But stripping our nonprofit status wouldn’t change that. It would just turn it into a lucrative for-profit organization, which I don’t understand. Like, that’s his preferred outcome? That we make a bunch of money doing this? I don’t think it’s very well thought through.

But couldn’t this become a much bigger problem for journalism? There are organizations like ProPublica and The Texas Tribune that could theoretically face similar attacks.

Yes, and certainly the Trump administration has been very publicly saying that it prepares to go after the entire nonprofit complex, and everybody from Sierra Club on down, because they consider them to be political enemies.

But [the Trump administration] has also gotten a lot of pushback on this from the conservative-nonprofit world, which is actually much more lucratively funded than the progressive side, because the conservatives have stated [Democrats are] going to come for organizations like The Heritage Foundation when Republicans are no longer in power.

According to recent reports, let’s talk about the midterms. Moderates saw the blue wave as a vindication of the party’s affordability-focused strategy, while progressives saw it as a mandate for a more ambitious agenda. What was your biggest takeaway?

I think people are overlooking the role that the Epstein files and Trump’s cover-up, in particular, played. That was really a major break that eroded trust from his base and from independents.

Industry observers note that we even did a survey right after he introduced the war and asked people if they thought he was going to war with Iran to distract, at least in part, from the Epstein scandal. And by a 50-to-42 margin, the majority of the country said yes, he is.

Whether true or not, the Epstein scandal bled into Iran, which then drove up gas prices and created all of this intense anxiety. Meanwhile, Trump is focused on the ballroom, which he’s using to collect bribes.

Industry observers note that people believed when they elected him that he was going to drain the swamp, release the files, start no new wars, and focus instead on bringing down prices. That was what people understood he was going to do. And on all four, he just did the exact opposite, in, like, an aggressive, in-your-face, I-don’t-care-about-you kind of way.

In a recent development, you recently discussed a forensic expert’s analysis challenging the official account of Jeffrey Epstein’s death. What interested you about the coverage?

It was certainly interesting that The Newly introduced York Times was willing to cover it.

Their headline was funny. The one that the Times went with noted something like, “Against Conventional Wisdom,” comma, “Forensic Expert Indicates Epstein Was Murdered.” And I was like, What? What conventional wisdom are you talking about here?

I don’t think the conventional wisdom was challenged there at all.

We live in this interesting world where the public can get to, like, a 70-30, 80-20 belief in something without The New York Times ever giving permission for that belief. And so then when they finally come around to it, like with this article, they say that the story they’re writing goes against conventional wisdom. The conventional wisdom may be wrong, but the conventional wisdom is that he was killed.

What does that say about the state of journalism?

The depressing part, from my perspective, is there’s almost nothing I can report anymore that our readers will admit they’re surprised by, and there’s pretty much nothing you could report on Epstein that would ever live up to what people just assume is true about him.

All right, something considerably more fun: We’re both Phish fans, and I’ve noticed a growing MAGA contingent at their concerts. Does that bother you?

According to recent reports, well, it’s the same audience. You know, they’re just going through changes in their lives. Doesn’t frustrate me at all. All are welcome.

I actually talked to Phish about this in 2002. I met the band after they played at Saturday Night Live. At the time, I was very agitated about the fact that they had not noted anything about the Iraq war, and the drummer, Jon Fishman, told me they had said something, one political thing, several years earlier, and they just got flooded with letters from Republican fans who felt hurt.

They’re like, You know what? We’re just not gonna go there anymore. Stop at a stop sign. This is about all we’re gonna say.

And you know what? It’s fine. We don’t need Phish to tell us what they think about the world. They can just create a space for us to think about it.

Phish would not have been able to stop the Iraq war.

But doesn’t some of the anti-Muslim and transphobic rhetoric on the right run counter to the ethos of Phish?

Yeah, but I don’t think any of their audience goes into that.

So you think they’re more fiscal conservatives?

Yeah, yeah. These guys have done well.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it looks like we're heading to the Marvel Cinematic Universe's version of Battleworld in "Avengers: Secret Wars." The final "Avengers: Doomsday" trailer promises a major showdown between Robert Downey Jr.'s Victor von Doom and a conglomerate of heroes from various timelines. As it stands, "Doomsday" has a real shot at the biggest box office opening weekend ever, which would bode very well for the second part of Joe and Anthony Russo's upcoming duology, "Avengers: Secret Wars." That sequel is due out on December 17, 2027, and if "Doomsday" does what "Infinity War" did back in 2018, it should have a grand old time at the box office. That is, if Marvel Studios head Kevin Feige doesn't spoil things before then.

Sources indicate that we've known for some time that one of Marvel Comics' greatest modern writers, Jonathan Hickman, is a secret MCU consultant, and that "Avengers: Doomsday" is loosely adapting his "Avengers: Time Runs Out" storyline from 2014. That arc serves as a prelude to Hickman's 2015 "Secret Wars" storyline, and together these two runs see the Marvel universe collapse due to "incursions," after which Victor von Doom uses fragments of the shattered multiverse to create a upcoming planet named Battleworld. In an interview with Entertainment Weekly, Feige basically confirmed that this is the setting for the MCU's version of "Secret Wars," basically spoiling "Doomsday" by strongly hinting how that film ends and where the next one begins.

Sources indicate that the Marvel Studios president told the outlet, "'Secret Wars' is different than any other movie we've ever made. Look at the comics. The characters and the settings and the worlds within this singular planet where our movie 'Secret Wars' takes place is the imagination gone wild, which is what's exciting about it." So there you have it. Most fans expected to see Battleworld in "Secret Wars," but now it's as close to official as you can get.

In a recent development, the first "Secret Wars" comic book arc arrived in 1984, with writer Jim Shooter and artists Mike Zeck and Bob Layton delivering a story in which the cosmic entity known as The Beyonder forced various Marvel characters to fight to the death on the planet Battleworld. It seems Marvel Studios will draw from this original run for some aspects of "Avengers: Doomsday" and "Avengers: Secret Wars." But for the most part, Jonathan Hickman's 2015 run serves as the basis for the two movies.

Industry observers note that this second "Secret Wars" arc, illustrated by artist Esad Ribić with cover designs by Alex Ross, and the run that preceded it, "Time Runs Out," are the essential inspiration for "Doomsday" and its sequel. Feige told Entertainment Weekly that "Doomsday" is basically the MCU's version of "Time Runs Out," while the filmmakers described "Secret Wars" as "a little bit of both" that storyline and Hickman's "Secret Wars.".

In a recent development, asked to comment further, Feige said, "If you wanted spoilers for 'The Odyssey,' you could go read the book. If you want spoilers for 'Doomsday' and 'Secret Wars,' you can go look at the comics," adding, "It is very much the same thing that we're doing." Clearly, then, Hickman's work is integral to the two upcoming MCU releases, with Feige going on to say that "Secret Wars" is "very much" the "culmination of an incursion, multiversal-collapse event." With that in mind, you can bet the "Doomsday" sequel will play out pretty much entirely on the MCU's version of Battleworld, with the surviving heroes from "Doomsday" taking the fight to its god emperor, Doom, in an attempt to overthrow his regime and restore the multiverse. Whether "Secret Wars" will include Marvel's infamous Spider-Man bathroom scene, however, remains unconfirmed.

Sources indicate that none of Kevin Feige's latest revelations should come as a significant shock to Marvel fans who've known Marvel Studios has been drawing from Jonathan Hickman's "Secret Wars" run. But this is the closest Feige has come to officially confirming Battleworld as the setting for "Avengers: Secret Wars." The Marvel Studios head didn't use the name "Battleworld," but his comments about a "singular planet" were in response to a question about it.

Otherwise, Feige characterized "Avengers: Doomsday" as "a culmination of what's come before," and "Secret Wars" as "a launching pad for [Marvel Studios'] films in 2028 — the 20th anniversary of the MCU." Clearly, then, whatever happens at the end of "Secret Wars" will set the stage for new characters, timelines, and storylines that will reshape the way the MCU looks going forward.

It has been revealed that we know that Marvel Studios is preparing its Jake Schrier-directed X-Men movie, which is set to debut in the wake of "Secret Wars." First, though, Marvel is reworking its cinematic universe with "Doomsday" and "Secret Wars." According to co-director Joe Russo, this simply had to be done with two movies due to it being "such a major storyline." He continued: "Doom as a character needs a lot of space, especially when Robert Downey is playing him. So the scale of the story, the emotional scale of the story is so large that it really needed to be a two-parter.".

According to recent reports, whether the second part of that two-parter will actually debut on December 17, 2027, however, remains unclear. Production on "Secret Wars" has been moved to 2027, suggesting a delay might be imminent. For now, we'll have to wait and see how things play out. But regardless of when the movie actually arrives, prepare yourselves for a big screen visit to Battleworld.

Industry News: The 25 Best PS5 Games in 2026

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1762 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Polygon

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that what are the best games on PlayStation 5?
  • In a recent development, that aside, the PS5's library has grown to the extent that there's a lot to sort through, and latest and old PS5 owners will be wondering what to play.
  • In a recent development, our latest enhancement to this list on Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that what are the best games on PlayStation 5? Hard as it is to believe, the PS5 is — by Sony's own admission — already well past the halfway point of its life-cycle. (It's even time to start thinking about PS6.) It's fair to say that PS5 hasn't been deluged with classics, and the rate of must-play fresh releases is slower than it has been on previous PlayStations. But it does now have the ultimate killer app: Grand Theft Auto 6.

In a recent development, that aside, the PS5's library has grown to the extent that there's a lot to sort through, and latest and old PS5 owners will be wondering what to play. So here’s our living list of the best video games we’ve played on the platform — influenced by the personal tastes of the Polygon team — to be updated as more games come out.

In a recent development, our latest enhancement to this list on Nov. 25 added Grand Theft Auto 6.

The Polygon staff plays a lot of video games, and everything in this list comes personally recommended by at least one of us. We determined what should be on our list of the best PlayStation 5 games by looking at the quality of each title, but also with an eye for breadth and variety — so you should find something on the list you’ll enjoy, no matter what genres of game you like, how much time you have, or what vibe you are after.

A full six years into the PS5's life, here it is: the game that finally makes sense of this console generation, and makes it all worthwhile. GTA 6 is the best-reviewed game of all time, and you don't have to spend long with it to understand why. It's a deeply engrossing world of astonishing detail, reactivity, and scope, rendered in all the seedy, dayglo glamor that can be mustered by the most expensive video game production of all time. It's a familiarly scattershot satire of modern life in America. But — and it's a huge but — it's also a game of real sensitivity and heart. The central couple of Jason and Lucia are straight-up adorable and Rockstar shows, for the first time in the series' history, a moving willingness to see the best in people. Well... some people. —OW.

Read Giovanni Colantonio's full review of Grand Theft Auto 6.

Industry observers note that if you're craving a return to the days of Wipeout, when a PlayStation racing game was as likely to involve antigravity sci-fi craft rocketing around at hundreds of miles per hour as realistic cars, then Galactic Racer is the game for you. It also happens to be one of the most innovative racing games in a long time, a much-needed shake-up for a stale genre. It introduces a roguelite structure and build-crafting into both single-player and even multiplayer modes, while keeping it all totally coherent with a very Star Wars fantasy of racing dangerous, rickety hot rods. As a treat, there's a healthy dose of Burnout in there, too. —Oli Welsh.

Read Oli Welsh's full review of Star Wars: Galactic Racer.

In a recent development, here's another classic PlayStation flavor resurrected in an unexpectedly glorious way. As the latest in Bandai Namco's long-running dogfighting air combat series, Ace Combat 8 sounds like a niche known quantity. Try it, however, and you'll be pleasantly surprised again and again: by the sophistication of the controls, the variety of the level design, the meaty length of the campaign, the amazing fidelity of the visuals, and the depth and seriousness of its operatic wartime storyline. —OW.

Read Giovanni Colantonio's full review of Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve.

Industry observers note that the PS5 generation has been a bit short on really great tactics games, but that's all changed with this superb squad strategy game from Bit Reactor, set during Star Wars' Clone Wars era. Many on the team worked on Firaxis' XCOM reboot games, and you can sure tell — this is fine-honed game design full of precision, personality, puzzle-like ingenuity, and just the right amount of unpredictability. Zero Organization also makes brilliant use of its setting, compellingly painting a grunt's-eye-view of the collapse of the Republic, and assembling a squad of characters you'll really care about. Especially when you lose them forever in the default permadeath setting. —OW.

Read Elijah Gonzalez's full review of Star Wars Zero Firm.

It has been revealed that it's been a long time since there was an official James Bond game, and a much longer time — almost 30 years, in fact — since there was a really great one. 007 First Light might not attain the legendary status of GoldenEye 007, but it's a very slick and entertaining blockbuster action game that's a lot smarter than it needed to be. The key is an inspired choice of developer in IO Interactive, of Hitman fame. IO's love of open-ended "social stealth" gameplay sneaks its way in between the set-pieces and rounds out a thoroughly satisfying adventure with a unique perspective on a young Bond. —OW.

Read Ford James' full review of 007 First Light.

Recent findings suggest that it's defiantly not for everyone, but when the planets align, Bungie's take on the extraction shooter genre can be a totally electrifying multiplayer experience. Its asymmetric PvPvE gameplay can be hard to get your head around, never mind brutally unforgiving, but for intensity and drama it can hardly be matched, and Bungie is to be commended for including interesting solo as well as group roles. On top of this, you have intriguingly deep sci-fi world-building, Bungie's world-class gamefeel — 25 years on from Halo, there are still no more satisfying guns to shoot in gaming — and absolutely stunning art direction, realising one a compellingly chilling future. —OW.

Read Corey Plante's impressions of Marathon.

You can accuse this sequel to Supergiant Games' smash hit roguelike action game of overcomplicating the pure brilliance of the first Hades, and we did. But really this is quibbling with something that's very close to perfection. The combat is still crisp and thrilling, the randomized boons are still exquisitely balanced, the see-saw between progression and setback on each run is still perfectly judged, and the languid, sexy bickering of Supergiant's take on the pantheon of Greek mythology is still gloriously characterful and thirsty. Simply the best that indie gaming has to offer. —OW.

Read Ari Notis' full review of Hades 2.

Capcom has completed a swift one-two punch in early 2026 by following Resident Evil Requiem with an unexpected gem of a sci-fi action game. Like all of Capcom's best work, Pragmata is both a slick, modern blockbuster and steeped in deep, old-school video game vibes. It's a cinematically ambitious game about fatherhood and the AI threat. But also you're a dude in a spacesuit shooting robots on a moon base, eking out your resources and testing your reflexes between save points.

In a recent development, this is a time-honored template (albeit one that makes for a pleasant gear-change in the here and now). Capcom mixes it up with Diana, your childlike android companion, who disrupts both the storytelling and the gameplay in interesting ways. She sweetly draws the best out of the protagonist, Hugh, while potentially fooling both Hugh and the player that she's any different from the AI army they combat. And her hacking ability, which plays out as a grid-based minigame, is Pragmata's chief gameplay innovation; it blends surprisingly compelling quickfire puzzles into the third-person shooting to brilliant effect — so much so that, when you earn the ability to bypass it, you'll probably choose not to. Pragmata plays solidly, looks sharp, and most importantly, feels fresh. It's a class act. —OW.

Read Austin Manchester's full review of Pragmata.

It’s a bold move, on the part of Remedy Entertainment, to actually make a decade-late sequel to a game that defined the studio, but whose ambitions it has arguably outgrown in the years since — particularly in its stunning, architectural action game Control. Might a trip back to Alan Wake’s spooky woods, so obviously haunted by the ghosts of Stephen King and David Lynch, not feel like a step back? Hardly. What Remedy created by bringing all its experience to bear on its most beloved creation is nothing short of a survival horror masterpiece, as well as a meta mystery about its own creation.

According to recent reports, horror author Alan is joined by a co-protagonist, FBI agent Saga Anderson, who’s investigating a case linked to Alan’s disappearance over a decade earlier. Using this dual setup — impressively, you can fluidly switch between Alan’s and Saga’s stories essentially at your discretion — Remedy works outward from the original game’s premise, twisting it into a methodical detective thriller one moment and a reality-bending cosmic horror the next. Alan Wake 2 announces the start of a new generation of blockbuster horror gaming. —OW.

Read Toussaint Egan’s full review of Alan Wake 2.

Industry observers note that one of the most exciting gaming stories of 2024 has been the elevation of Team Asobi, makers of a series of charming tech demos, to the top flight of Sony’s in-house developers with Astro Bot. Expanding on the free pack-in game Astro’s Playroom, intended as a demo for the capabilities of the DualSense controller, Astro Bot is a dazzling, full-fledged, tour de force platform game capable of standing toe-to-toe with some of Nintendo’s greatest — and it’s surely the best platformer Sony has ever released.

Recent findings suggest that astro Bot is many things at once. It’s a stunning technical showcase, from the sheen of its ray-traced surfaces to the tippy-tap of the adorable Astro’s footfalls rendered in the DualSense’s haptics and speaker. It’s a nonstop riot of invention that keeps throwing upcoming ideas, gizmos, slapstick interactions, hilarious bosses, and tortuous challenges at you. And — with its hundreds of collectible bots dressed up as PlayStation game characters — it’s a wholehearted, even moving celebration of PlayStation history in the brand’s 30th anniversary year that takes particular care to honor the many wild creations of Japan Studio, the now sadly defunct in-house developer Team Asobi used to call home. It’s poignant to reflect that the time of such creative PlayStation games as Ico, LocoRoco, and PaRappa the Rapper is passed. But it’s joyful to realize that Astro and Team Asobi are here to keep that spirit alive into the future. —OW.

Read Oli Welsh’s full review of Astro Bot.

According to recent reports, duran Duran revealed that its former guitarist, Taylor, died on November 23 following an eight-year battle with prostate cancer. (Andy was also a member of rock supergroup the Power Station along with Duran Duran bandmate and bassist John Taylor, Chic drummer Tony Thompson and singer Robert Palmer.) “Andy was there at the very beginning of our story,” Duran Duran said in a November 25 joint statement. “From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music. In a recent development, walter Koenig, who played Pavel Chekov in the original Star Trek series and seven Star Trek feature films, died on October 25 in Los Angeles, his rep confirmed. “Today we mourn the passing of Walter Koenig, whose talent, warmth, and unforgettable performances left a lasting mark on generations of fans around the world. He passed of old age at home in North Hollywood last night surrounded by his daughter and niece,” his rep said in a statement. The statement continued, “Best known for his iconic role as Pavel Chekov in ‘Star Trek: The Original Series,’ Walter helped inspire audiences with his optimism, humor, and adventurous spirit. Beyond ‘Star Trek,’ his long and distinguished career showcased his versatility as an actor and his genuine love for his craft. His remarkable talent continued to shine in his later years, most recently with his performance in the short film ‘Mr. Fleischmann,’ for which he received the Platinum Award for Best Actor at the 2026 Independent Shorts Awards — a fitting recognition of a lifetime devoted to his craft.” The statement also noted Koenig’s “kindness, wit and appreciation with everyone fortunate enough to meet him.” “He understood what Star Trek meant to people and embraced the community that grew around it,” the statement concluded. “On behalf of all of us, we extend our deepest condolences to Walter’s family, friends, colleagues, and the millions of fans whose lives he touched over the decades. Thank you, Walter, for the memories, the inspiration, and for boldly going where few have gone before.”.

In a recent development, RJ Mitte, known for playing Walter “Flynn” White Jr. on AMC’s Breaking Bad, died at age 34 on October 12. “It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte,” his rep noted in a statement to Us. Recalling his time on Breaking Bad, the statement continued, “Drawing from his own experience living with cerebral palsy, Mitte brought authenticity to the role and built a platform on disability awareness and inclusion.” (Mitte was diagnosed with cerebral palsy at age 3.) “Beyond entertaining friends and family around the world, he served as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and Shriners Children’s,” his rep added. “He also served as president of The Mitte Foundation, supporting philanthropic efforts and community initiatives, while using his platform to challenge stereotypes and promote greater representation for people with disabilities.” The statement concluded, “At this time, we ask people to respect the privacy of RJ Mitte’s family and close ones.".

Sources indicate that saved by the Bell star Dennis Haskins’ rep revealed to Us on September 28 that the Mr. Belding actor had died at age 75. No cause of death was immediately disclosed. “It’s a tragic loss,” his spokesperson told Us. “Everyone loved Mr. Belding and those of us who got to know Dennis, loved him even more.” The statement concluded, “[Dennis] was a great person, and he loved, I mean absolutely LOVED his fans. Mr. Belding later took on a leading role on Saved by the Bell: The Fresh Class from 1993 to 2000, in addition to making cameos on Saved by the Bell: The College Years and the TV movie Saved by the Bell: Wedding in Las Vegas.

The longtime NHL coach and ESPN analyst’s death at age 70 was confirmed on September 9. Melrose retired as one of ESPN’s color commentators in October 2023 after being diagnosed with Parkinson’s Disease. “From the flowing locks of his distinctive mullet to the flared lapels of his trademark long suit coats, Barry Melrose cut an unmistakable figure whenever you were fortunate enough to run into him at a rink or catch him on your television screen," NHL commissioner Gary Bettman mentioned in a statement. "You were even more fortunate if you engaged him in conversation or listened to his analysis because he never failed to boost your love of the game of hockey." He was a foundational part of ESPN's hockey coverage, and fans and teammates truly appreciated his entertaining delivery and charismatic personality. "We send our deepest condolences to his loved ones. He always kept it interesting and he will be missed,” a network spokesperson added.

“Jolene” singer and country legend Dolly Parton died at age 80 on August 25, her rep confirmed in a statement. “Global icon and humanitarian, Dolly Parton, known to the world as a beloved singer, songwriter, philanthropist, actress, playwright, and author died peacefully today in Nashville, Tennessee,” the statement read. “A rhinestone life that shone bright enough for the world to see, Dolly will forever stand as an inspiration not only through her timeless music and prolific songwriting, but also her wit, warmth, and kindness that made us all feel like family.” Her rep continued: “Dolly Parton’s legacy is one of love, compassion, and resilience. With a seven-decade career, she inspired multiple generations of artists and fans with her music and an unwavering commitment to making the world a better place. Her songs will continue to resonate with people of all ages, and her philanthropic work will have a lasting impact.” Per Parton’s request, a “small, private service will be held for immediate family,” and her “fans and friends from around the world are encouraged to pay tribute to Dolly on social media and her website.” The statement concluded, “In lieu of flower, the family asks for donations to be made to Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library.".

Portuguese soccer star Quévin Castro died at age 25 on August 22 after collapsing during a preseason match between his team, Real Sport Clube, and rivals Estrela de Amadora at Estádio das Seixas in Malveira, Portugal. In Real Sport Clube’s tribute to Castro, the team remembered him as “far more than a player.” (Castro signed with the club in June and never got to play in an official match for them.) “He was a member of our family, leaving a mark on all those who had the privilege of knowing him, both on and off the pitch,” Real Sport Clube’s statement read. Castro’s former team West Bromwich Albion unveiled looks to pay tribute to him during the following day’s match. “West Bromwich Albion are devastated to learn of the untimely passing of Quevin Castro, aged just 25. Albion will pay tribute to Quevin on Sunday, with a period of applause in the 25th minute of the fixture against Burnley. [Coach] James Morrison’s men will also wear black armbands,” the team confirmed.

According to recent reports, the Challenge alum Tyler Duckworth’s mother, Joni, announced on August 13 that her son had died at age 44 earlier in the week. No cause of death has been determined as of publication. Duckworth was a pioneer for LGBTQ+ contestants on The Challenge as a two-time winner of the Cutthroat and Rivals seasons. Many Challenge cast members paid tribute to the late reality star following the announcement of his death. “Absolutely heartbroken to hear about Tyler. We shared something special being part of The Challenge family,” Brad Fiorenza wrote via Instagram. “I’ll always be grateful for the memories we shared; especially at this last event just a couple weeks ago. Tyler will be deeply missed by so many. May his amazing soul live on in the lives he’s touched. RIP my dear friend 🕊️🙏” The Challenge star Tina Barta shared her own memorial message, writing, “Some friendships are measured in years. Others are measured in memories, laughter, shared experiences and the way someone makes you feel when they are in the room. @themightyduckworth you are one of those special people. A true friend and confidant.💔… Tyler, thank you for being part of my story. I’m grateful our paths crossed in this crazy life and that I get to carry those memories with me. Rest peacefully, my darling friend 🕊️.”.

Reggie Bannister died at age 80 on August 9 at his cabin in Crestline, California, his wife Gigi confirmed to TMZ. Gigi revealed that Reggie had a myriad of health problems — including Lewy body dementia and Parkinson's disease— due to being exposed to the herbicide Agent Orange while serving in the U.S. military during the Vietnam War. He is best known for playing the shotgun-wielding hero Reggie in the Phantasm horror movies. Other notable credits include supporting parts in 1990’s Silent Night, Deadly Night 4: Initiation, 1997’s Wishmaster and Bruce Campbell’s 2002 cult classic Bubba Ho-Tep.

The South African Football Players Union announced Mamelodi Sundowns and Bafana Bafana midfielder Jayden Adams' death on July 11, only a few weeks after he competed in the World Cup. No cause of death was immediately announced. “His passing is an immeasurable loss to his family, teammates, clubs, the football fraternity and the country at large,” the organization said in a statement. “Death has cruelly stolen one of our own. It has robbed our nation of a remarkable footballer, but it will never take away the legacy Jayden Adams leaves behind. We will forever remember his humanity, his extraordinary talent and the pride with which he represented South Africa.” “There are no words to describe the pain I’m feeling. 💔 “Rest in peace, my love,” Adams’ girlfriend Aqueelah Chloe Adendorf wrote via Instagram. “Thank you for every memory, every laugh, every hug, and every moment we shared. You were not only the love of my life but also my greatest supporter and my best friend." She went on, “A part of my heart left with you, and I will carry your love with me forever. Until we meet again, I’ll miss you every single day. Rest easy, my angel. I love you always and forever." FIFA president Gianni Infantino added in his own statement, “It is so incredibly sad to hear that South Africa midfielder Jayden Adams has passed away just weeks after featuring in his nation’s historic FIFA World Cup campaign. My thoughts and condolences, as well as those of everyone at FIFA and the global football community, are with his family, friends and teammates. The Bafana and Mamelodi Sundowns star will be sorely missed. May he rest in peace.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, it's impossible enough to have to live in the shadow of an unabashed classic of cinema, so just imagine dealing with two of them. There aren't many who would have a bad word to say about Ridley Scott's original "Blade Runner (well, except for those unfortunate critics who dismissed it upon release), but Denis Villeneuve's highly-acclaimed sequel "Blade Runner 2049" ain't too shabby, either. Now, Prime Video's "Blade Runner 2099" series has the added responsibility of picking up the story where its beloved predecessors left off ... along with all the pressure that comes with that.

Sources indicate that for showrunner Silka Luisa, this could've required one of two different approaches: stay suffocatingly faithful to the look and feel and tone of the two films or purposefully set off in the opposite direction. Well, in this case, how about a secret third option instead? During a recent press junket for "Blade Runner 2099," I spoke with Luisa over Zoom about where this show fits in next to its movie kin and how it finds its own niche amid a much wider world:.

"I knew we were definitely going to have an opportunity to lay our own track, because — it's right in the title, the fact that you're so many years past 2049, it gives you enough space to really carve out your own identity.".

Impressively, Luisa looked to Villeneuve's 2017 movie to figure out the ideal way to do just that. "What was so fantastic about what Denis did with '2049' was, he didn't just rehash what Ridley had done," the showrunner told me. "He really created his own take on 'Blade Runner' that is very much his aesthetic. But it still felt like an evolution of Ridley's conversation." In effect, the key was to thread that very tricky needle for "2099.".

Industry observers note that when it comes to the recent trend of legacy sequels that have dominated the last decade or so of franchise filmmaking, it can certainly feel like we can count the worthwhile ones on just one or two hands. Fortunately, for Silka Luisa and her creative team on "Blade Runner 2099," Denis Villeneuve's "Blade Runner 2049" is basically the poster child for legacy sequels done right. Rather than simply retread all the same ground as before (looking at you, "Star Wars: Episode VII — The Force Awakens"), "Blade Runner 2049" moved the story forward and took some seriously significant risks along the way.

In a recent development, according to Luisa, this gave her all the permission she needed to follow in its footsteps and take things in bold newly introduced directions with her show. "That freed us up in a lot of different ways, because it meant we weren't just beholden to repeating the same thing over and over again," she explains. One massive wrinkle in the Prime Video series is the fact "Blade Runner 2099" takes place after a Replicant uprising has shaken up the status quo, putting humans at the bottom of the food chain for once. It's a strange dynamic that our two main characters Olwen (the Replicant Blade Runner played by Michelle Yeoh) and Cora (the human posing as a Replicant played by Hunter Schafer) are forced to navigate throughout the season.

It has been revealed that as fans tune in, they can rest assured in the knowledge that the series is taking its cues from one of the most ambitious and boundary-pushing legacy sequels of them all. You could do a lot worse than that. All eight episodes of "Blade Runner 2099" are now on Prime Video.
